# Proof of P4

We use P1 exactly as supplied. No external paper is used. All logarithms are natural. Constants introduced below depend only on $f$, except for the absolute constant supplied by P1.

## Polynomial bounds and a periodic averaging lemma

The leading coefficient of $f$ is positive: otherwise $f(t)\geq 2$ for all $t\geq 1$ would fail. Since $f(t)>0$ on this interval, continuity and the positive limit of $f(t)/t^d$ give constants $a>0$ and $B\geq 1$ such that, for every $t\geq 1$,
\[
 a t^d\leq f(t)\leq B t^d,
 \qquad |f'(t)|\leq B t^{d-1}.
 \tag{1}
\]
When $d\geq 2$, enlarge $B$ so that
\[
 |f''(t)|\leq B t^{d-2}\quad(t\geq 1).
 \tag{2}
\]
When $d=1$, $f''=0$. Define
\[
 U=\frac{B}{a},\qquad
 V=\frac{B}{a}+\frac{B^2}{a^2},\qquad D=U+V.
 \tag{3}
\]
For $w(t)=f'(t)/f(t)$, equations (1)--(2), including $f''=0$ when $d=1$, imply
\[
 0<w(t)\leq\frac{U}{t},\qquad
 |w'(t)|
 \leq\frac{|f''(t)|}{f(t)}+\frac{|f'(t)|^2}{f(t)^2}
 \leq\frac{V}{t^2}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Also $f'(t)\geq 1$ and $f(1)\geq 2$ give $f(t)\geq t+1$. Thus $y<x$, and
\[
 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \leq U\sum_{1\leq k\leq y}\frac1k
 \leq U(1+\log y)
 \leq 2U\log(2x).
 \tag{5}
\]
Here the sum has at most $\lfloor y\rfloor\leq\lfloor x\rfloor$ terms; the harmonic-sum bound follows by comparison with the integral of $1/t$ on $[1,y]$.

We will use the following elementary lemma. If $b(k)$ is periodic of integer period $r\geq 1$, satisfies $|b(k)|\leq 1$, and has mean
\[
 m=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r b(a),
\]
then, for real $1\leq u\leq v$ and a continuously differentiable function $F$ on $[u,v]$,
\[
 \left|\sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^v F(t)\,dt\right|
 \leq 4r\left(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\,dt\right).
 \tag{6}
\]
To prove this, put
\[
 P(t)=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}b(k)-mt.
\]
Writing $t=qr+s$, where $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\leq s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel. The remaining sum has at most $r$ terms of modulus at most $1$, and $|ms|\leq r$. Hence $|P(t)|\leq 2r$. Consequently
\[
 D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\leq t}b(k)-m(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)
 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad |D_u(t)|\leq 4r.
\]
Integration by parts gives the exact identity
\[
 \sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^vF(t)\,dt
 =F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\,dt,
\]
which proves (6), with the indicated convention at both endpoints.

For later use, (4) and (6) yield
\[
 \left|\sum_{z<k\leq y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
       -m\log(Y/Z)\right|
 \leq \frac{4Dr}{z}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, $|w(y)|\leq U/z$, while
\(
\int_z^y |w'(t)|\,dt\leq V/z.
\)
These bounds also cover $z=y$; in that case the two conclusions of P4 are immediate. We may henceforth take $z<y$.

## Spectral notation and the common density

Let $c_r(n)$, $\gamma(r)$, and $\lambda(r)$ have the meanings in P1. Since
\(
\lambda(r)=\varphi(r)\gamma(r)^2
\)
and $c_r(n)$ is a sum of $\varphi(r)$ complex numbers of modulus $1$,
\[
 |c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
 \mathfrak S(n)=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)}.
 \tag{8}
\]
In particular, P1 gives absolute convergence, uniformly in $n\geq 1$, because $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.

For $h\geq 1$, define
\[
 \beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r
           \frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)}.
 \tag{9}
\]
Thus $|\beta_r(h)|\leq 1$, and
\[
 \mathcal W(h):=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)
 \tag{10}
\]
converges absolutely and uniformly in $h\geq 1$. We now prove that
\[
 \mathcal W(h)=W_f(h).
 \tag{11}
\]

For completeness, the elementary Ramanujan-sum identities needed here follow directly from finite sums. Inserting
\(
\mathbf 1_{(a,r)=1}=\sum_{b\mid(a,r)}\mu(b)
\)
into the definition of $c_r(n)$, and summing the resulting geometric progression, gives
\[
 c_r(n)
 =\sum_{b\mid r}\mu(b)
       \sum_{a'=1}^{r/b}\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i a'n}{r/b}\right)
 =\sum_{s\mid(r,n)}s\mu(r/s).
 \tag{12}
\]
Factoring this divisor sum over two coprime moduli shows that $c_{rs}(n)=c_r(n)c_s(n)$ when $(r,s)=1$. The Chinese remainder theorem, applied to the complete average in (9), therefore gives
\[
 \beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)\quad((r,s)=1).
 \tag{13}
\]
Here we also use $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$, which follows by counting invertible residue classes under the same bijection.

The function $\lambda(r)/c^2$ is multiplicative, is supported on integers with no prime cube divisor, and has prime-power values
\[
 \frac{\lambda(p)}{c^2}=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
 \frac{\lambda(p^2)}{c^2}=\frac{p^2-p}{(p^2-1)^2}.
 \tag{14}
\]
The absolute convergence in (10) and (13)--(14) permit its Euler product. Equations (12) give, for each integer $n$,
\[
 c_p(n)=p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}-1,
 \qquad
 c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n},
\]
and hence
\[
 c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
 \tag{15}
\]
Put
\[
 \delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
\]
The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ can also be taken modulo $p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. It follows from (14)--(15) that the local factor, before including the local factor of $c^2$, is
\[
 1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}
 =1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}.
 \tag{16}
\]

Write $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$. If $j=2$, the condition is $p^2\mid f(a)$, so there are $\rho(p^2)$ classes modulo $p^2$. If $j=1$, the condition is $p\mid f(a)$, and each of its $\rho(p)$ classes modulo $p$ has $p$ lifts modulo $p^2$. If $j=0$, every class is allowed. Using $\rho(1)=1$, the three cases give
\[
 \delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^j)}{p^j},\qquad 0\leq\delta_p(h)\leq 1.
 \tag{17}
\]
No restriction on the coefficients of $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.

Unique factorization and the absolutely convergent geometric series for each prime give
\(
c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2.
\)
Multiplying (16) by its local factor gives the exact identity
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (1-p^{-2})^2
 \left(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}\\
 &=(1-2p^{-2})
       \left(1+\frac{\rho(p^{j_p(h)})}
       {p^{j_p(h)}(p^2-2)}\right).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{18}
\]
This proves (11). All product rearrangements are absolute: the deviation from $1$ of the first expression on the right of (18) is at most $2/p^2$, and the added term in the second factor is at most
\(
1/(p^2-2)\leq 2/p^2.
\)
The sum of these bounds over primes is finite. This proves the asserted absolute convergence of $W_f(h)$. For the product defining $\mathfrak S(n)$, its local factor is
$1-2/p^2+\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}/p^2$, whose deviation from $1$ is at most $2/p^2$; its product therefore converges absolutely as well. Finally,
\[
 0\leq\frac{\rho(r)}r\leq 1,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
 \leq\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)=c,
 \tag{19}
\]
which proves absolute convergence of $R_f$.

For real $R\geq 2$, set
\[
 L_R=(\log(2R))^2,\qquad
 T_R=\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r),\qquad
 M_R=\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r).
\]
By P1 there is an absolute $C_0>0$ such that
\[
 T_R\leq C_0R^{-1/2}L_R,
 \qquad M_R\leq C_0R^{1/2}L_R.
 \tag{20}
\]

## The first averaging assertion

For each positive integer $r$, the sequence
\(
b(k)=\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
\)
has period $r$, modulus at most $1$, and mean $\rho(r)/r$. Thus (7) gives
\[
 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
 =\frac{\rho(r)}r\log(Y/Z)+e_r,
 \qquad |e_r|\leq\frac{4Dr}{z}.
 \tag{21}
\]
The first identity for the squared densities in P1 applies to $q=f(k)$, which is a positive integer. Therefore, writing the expression to be estimated as $S_1$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_1
 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}f'(k)\sum_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)^2\\
 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
                     \sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{22}
\]
The part in (22) with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most
\[
 T_R\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \leq 2U T_R\log(2x)
 \tag{23}
\]
by (5). This uses at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$; before summing, the bound for each such value is $T_R f'(k)/f(k)\leq U T_R/k$.

For $r\leq R$, there are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices. Before summing, the error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ in (21) is at most $4Dr\lambda(r)/z$. After summing it is at most $4DM_R/z$. Equations (21)--(23) consequently give
\[
 \left|S_1-\log(Y/Z)\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r\right|
 \leq\frac{4DM_R}{z}+2U T_R\log(2x).
 \tag{24}
\]
For the infinite omitted part of the density coefficient, (19) gives the bound $\lambda(r)\log(Y/Z)$ at each index $r>R$, and summing gives
\[
 \log(Y/Z)\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
 \leq T_R\log(2x),
 \tag{25}
\]
since $2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x$. As $Z\leq Bz^d$, we have
\(
z^{-1}\leq B^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}.
\)
Combining (20), (24), and (25) proves the explicit bound
\[
 \boxed{
 |S_1-R_f\log(Y/Z)|
 \leq C_0\left(
 4DB^{1/d} Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
 \right).}
 \tag{26}
\]

## A weight bound for the second assertion

Let
\[
 H=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{Z}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since $f'(t)\geq 1$, $f$ has a continuous increasing inverse on $[f(1),\infty)$. For $1\leq h\leq H$, define
\[
 v_h=\min\{y,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad
 F_h(t)=f'(t)(x-hf(t))\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
 \tag{27}
\]
These definitions are valid because $x/h\geq Z=f(z)$. They give
\[
 z\leq v_h\leq (x/(ah))^{1/d},\qquad
 0\leq x-hf(t)\leq x\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
 \tag{28}
\]
Define a constant $K$ by
\[
 K=
 \begin{cases}
 B+B^2/a,&d=1,\\[2mm]
 B+B/(d-1)+B^2/((2d-1)a),&d\geq 2.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{29}
\]
We claim
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 \leq Kxv_h^{d-1}.
 \tag{30}
\]
For $d\geq 2$, (1)--(2) and (28) give
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bxv_h^{d-1},
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 &\leq\int_z^{v_h}
       \left(|f''(t)|(x-hf(t))+h|f'(t)|^2\right)\,dt\\
 &\leq Bx\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\,dt
       +hB^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\,dt\\
 &\leq\frac{B}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}
       +\frac{hB^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1}\\
 &\leq\left(\frac{B}{d-1}+\frac{B^2}{(2d-1)a}\right)
          xv_h^{d-1}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{31}
\]
The last inequality uses $hv_h^d\leq x/a$, from (28). For $d=1$, $f''=0$ gives
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bx,\qquad
 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 \leq hB^2(v_h-z)\leq hB^2v_h\leq B^2x/a.
 \tag{32}
\]
Thus (30) holds for every $d\geq 1$.

Apply (6) to
\(
b(k)=c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)
\)
with mean $\beta_r(h)$. This sequence has period $r$ because $f$ has integer coefficients. Equations (28)--(30) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left|\sum_{z<k\leq v_h}
     f'(k)(x-hf(k))\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}
   -\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du\right|\\
 &\hspace{15mm}\leq
 4Kr x v_h^{d-1}
 \leq 4K a^{-(d-1)/d} r x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{33}
\]
If $v_h=z$, the left side is zero and this bound still applies.

The $h$-sum has exactly $H\leq x/Z$ indices. The bound in (33) is the bound before summing. To sum it, the function $t^{-1+1/d}$ is nonincreasing and integrable on $(0,H]$, and therefore
\[
 \sum_{h=1}^{H}h^{-1+1/d}
 \leq\int_0^H t^{-1+1/d}\,dt
 =dH^{1/d}\leq d(x/Z)^{1/d}.
 \tag{34}
\]
This includes $d=1$, when the first inequality is equality. Combining (33)--(34), the error after summing over $h$ is at most
\[
 K_2 r x^2 Z^{-1/d},\qquad
 K_2=4Kd\,a^{-(d-1)/d}.
 \tag{35}
\]
In particular no logarithm is introduced by this sum.

## The second averaging assertion

Define the finite approximations
\[
 \mathfrak S_R(n)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)
                         \frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad
 W_R(h)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
\]
Equations (8)--(11) give, uniformly for positive integers $n,h$,
\[
 |\mathfrak S(n)-\mathfrak S_R(n)|\leq T_R,
 \qquad |W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\leq T_R.
 \tag{36}
\]

Let $S_2$ denote the discrete expression in the second assertion and $I_2$ its integral expression. Define $S_{2,R}$ and $I_{2,R}$ by replacing $\mathfrak S$ and $W_f$ with $\mathfrak S_R$ and $W_R$, respectively.

For a fixed integer $k$ with $z<k\leq y$, there are
\(
H_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\leq x/f(k)
\)
indices $h$. Before summing over $h$, the error from (36) is at most $T_R f'(k)(x-hf(k))\leq T_R x f'(k)$. After summing over these $H_k$ indices, it is at most
\(
T_R x^2 f'(k)/f(k).
\)
Summing this last bound over at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$ and using (5) gives
\[
 |S_2-S_{2,R}|\leq 2U T_R x^2\log(2x).
 \tag{37}
\]
For each $t\in[Z,Y]$, the $h$-sum has $\lfloor x/t\rfloor\leq x/t$ indices. Before summing, the error in an integrand term is at most $T_R(x-ht)\leq T_R x$. After summing it is at most $T_R x^2/t$. Integration gives
\[
 |I_2-I_{2,R}|
 \leq T_R x^2\int_Z^Y\frac{dt}{t}
 =T_R x^2\log(Y/Z)
 \leq T_R x^2\log(2x).
 \tag{38}
\]

It remains to compare the finite approximations. All relevant sums are finite, so their orders can be interchanged. The change of variables $t=f(u)$ gives, for each $h\leq H$,
\[
 \int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du
 =\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\,dt.
 \tag{39}
\]
Moreover, for integer $k$ in $(z,y]$, the condition $h\leq x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\leq v_h$. Thus (35) compares the entire $h$-sum at a fixed $r$ in $S_{2,R}$ with its counterpart in $I_{2,R}$. Before summing over $r$, its error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ is at most
\(
K_2r\lambda(r)x^2 Z^{-1/d}.
\)
There are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices $r\leq R$; after summing, (20) gives
\[
 |S_{2,R}-I_{2,R}|
 \leq K_2x^2Z^{-1/d}M_R
 \leq C_0K_2 x^2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R.
 \tag{40}
\]
Combining (20) and (37)--(40) proves
\[
 \boxed{
 |S_2-I_2|
 \leq C_0 x^2\left(
 K_2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
 \right).}
 \tag{41}
\]

Finally, set
\[
 C(f)=C_0\max\{4DB^{1/d},\ K_2,\ 2U+1\}.
\]
With $A$ as in the statement, (26) is the first asserted inequality with right side $C(f)A$, and (41) is the second with right side $C(f)x^2A$. All constants are independent of $x,z,y,R$. Every estimate above is valid on the full stated ranges, including $d=1$ and polynomials with arbitrary content, discriminant, or factorization.

## Numerical sanity checks and source record

A Python check using exact rational arithmetic verified (18) for $p=2,3,5,7,11$ and each of the test densities $0,p^{-2},p^{-1},1$. A separate floating-point check verified the bound (34) for $d=1,\ldots,8$ and $H=1,2,10,1000$. These checks were only sanity checks; (18) and (34) were proved algebraically and by integration above.

The only assumed proposition is the supplied P1. No published source or other run's artifacts were consulted; no excluded source was encountered. There were no supplied objections or previous-proof artifacts for this attempt.

1	# Proof of P3
2	
3	We prove the stronger bound
4	\[
5	\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
6	\tag{1}
7	\]
8	with an absolute constant \(K\), for all the parameters in the statement.
9	The argument is elementary and does not require a circle-method cutoff.
10	No external sources or results from the supplied papers are used, and the
11	dependency P1 is not needed. No numerical checks are used.
12	
13	## An explicit divisor bound
14	
15	Write \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors of a positive integer
16	\(n\). Define the absolute constant
17	\[
18	D=\prod_{p<2^{10}}(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2},
19	\]
20	where the product is over primes. We will use
21	\[
22	\tau(n)\le Dn^{1/10}\qquad(n\ge1).
23	\tag{2}
24	\]
25	Here is an elementary verification. For every integer \(a\ge0\),
26	\(a+1\le2^a\), as follows by induction. Consequently, if \(p\ge2^{10}\),
27	then \(a+1\le p^{a/10}\). If \(p<2^{10}\), the geometric-series identity gives
28	\[
29	(a+1)p^{-a/10}
30	\le\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)p^{-j/10}
31	=(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2}.
32	\]
33	Multiplication over the prime powers in the factorization of \(n\) proves
34	(2); the factors included in \(D\) but absent from this factorization are
35	all at least one.
36	
37	We also record the following bounds for positive real \(t\ge1\) and positive
38	integers \(H\):
39	\[
40	\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}\le2,\qquad
41	\sum_{j>H}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac1H,\qquad
42	\sum_{j>t}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac2t,\qquad
43	\sum_{j=1}^{H}\frac1j\le1+\log H.
44	\tag{3}
45	\]
46	The first, second and fourth inequalities follow by comparison with the
47	integrals of \(u^{-2}\) and \(u^{-1}\). For the third, put \(k=\lfloor t\rfloor\).
48	Then \(k\ge t/2\), so the second inequality gives a bound \(1/k\le2/t\).
49	
50	## Truncating the square-divisor identities
51	
52	Fix real \(x\ge2\) and an integer \(1\le m\le x\), and put
53	\[
54	L=x-m\ge0,\qquad H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor.
55	\]
56	In particular,
57	\[
58	\tfrac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}.
59	\tag{4}
60	\]
61	For positive integers \(k\), define
62	\[
63	T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\le H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d),\qquad
64	R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d).
65	\]
66	All divisor variables in this proof are positive integers. The identity
67	\[
68	\mu^2(k)=\sum_{d^2\mid k}\mu(d)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)
69	\tag{5}
70	\]
71	follows by multiplying the local factors: a prime occurring to exponent at
72	least two contributes \(1+\mu(p)=0\); if no such prime occurs, the sum is one.
73	Also
74	\[
75	|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k),\qquad
76	|R_H(k)|\le\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}1.
77	\tag{6}
78	\]
79	
80	For either of the two sets
81	\[
82	I_0=\{n:1\le n\le L\},\qquad
83	I_m=\{n+m:1\le n\le L\},
84	\]
85	there are \(\lfloor L\rfloor\) elements, all positive integers at most \(x\).
86	For each fixed \(d\), the number of elements divisible by \(d^2\) is at most
87	\(\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor\le x/d^2\). The outer sum below has
88	\(\max(0,\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor-H)\le\sqrt x\) terms. Thus (3) and (6) give,
89	for each \(I\in\{I_0,I_m\}\),
90	\[
91	\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
92	\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
93	\le\frac{x}{H}.
94	\tag{7}
95	\]
96	This estimate also holds when either set is empty.
97	
98	The exact product identity
99	\[
100	\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)
101	=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
102	\]
103	and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
104	most
105	\[
106	|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
107	\]
108	where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
109	\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
110	each of its two terms, yields
111	\[
112	\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
113	\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
114	\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
115	\tag{8}
116	\]
117	In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).
118	
119	## Counting the truncated congruences
120	
121	For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
122	\[
123	n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
124	\]
125	are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
126	both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
127	the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
128	\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
129	\[
130	a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
131	\]
132	Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
133	\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
134	\[
135	h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
136	\]
137	For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
138	number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
139	\[
140	\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
141	-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
142	=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
143	\tag{9}
144	\]
145	This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).
146	
147	Define
148	\[
149	A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
150	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
151	\]
152	Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
153	\[
154	\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
155	\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
156	\tag{10}
157	\]
158	Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
159	at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
160	most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.
161	
162	## The infinite main term and its uniform tail
163	
164	Consider
165	\[
166	A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
167	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
168	\]
169	This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
170	with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
171	absolute sum by
172	\[
173	\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
174	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
175	   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
176	   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
177	\le8.
178	\tag{11}
179	\]
180	
181	We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
182	\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
183	\[
184	\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
185	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
186	  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
187	  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
188	\tag{12}
189	\]
190	For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
191	\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
192	and their total is at most
193	\[
194	\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
195	\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
196	\]
197	For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
198	\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
199	\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
200	\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
201	bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
202	\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
203	bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
204	\[
205	|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
206	=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
207	\tag{13}
208	\]
209	All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
210	\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).
211	
212	Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
213	one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
214	finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
215	exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
216	For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
217	follows:
218	
219	| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
220	| --- | --- | --- |
221	| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
222	| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
223	| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
224	| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |
225	
226	It follows that
227	\[
228	\begin{aligned}
229	A(m)
230	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
231	                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
232	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
233	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
234	  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
235	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
236	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
237	=\mathfrak S(m).
238	\end{aligned}
239	\tag{14}
240	\]
241	The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
242	because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.
243	
244	## Combining the bounds
245	
246	Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
247	\[
248	\begin{aligned}
249	L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
250	&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
251	&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
252	&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
253	\end{aligned}
254	\tag{15}
255	\]
256	For \(x\ge1\),
257	\[
258	\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
259	\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
260	=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
261	\]
262	Thus (15) is at most
263	\[
264	32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
265	\tag{16}
266	\]
267	Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
268	\[
269	\begin{aligned}
270	\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
271	&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
272	&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
273	\end{aligned}
274	\]
275	This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
276	\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
277	\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
278	\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
279	uniformity. \(\square\)
280

\[
\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
\tag{1}
\]

\]

\[

\]

\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
\le\frac{x}{H}.
\tag{7}
\]

\[

=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
\]
and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
most
\[
|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
\]
where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
each of its two terms, yields
\[
\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
\tag{8}
\]
In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).

## Counting the truncated congruences

For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
\[
n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
\[
a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
\]
Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
\[
h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
\]
For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
\tag{9}
\]
This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).

Define
\[
A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
\[
\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.

## The infinite main term and its uniform tail

Consider
\[
A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
absolute sum by
\[
\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
\le8.
\tag{11}
\]

We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
\[
\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
\tag{12}
\]
For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
and their total is at most
\[
\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
\]
For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
\[
|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
\tag{13}
\]
All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).

Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
follows:

| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |

It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(m)
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
=\mathfrak S(m).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.

## Combining the bounds

Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
For \(x\ge1\),
\[
\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
\]
Thus (15) is at most
\[
32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
\tag{16}
\]
Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
uniformity. \(\square\)

1	# Proof of P6
2	
3	We use P5 as a black box, with the notation in `statement.md` and
4	`deps/P5.md`. In particular,
5	\[
6	D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\qquad(\Re s>-3/4),
7	\tag{1}
8	\]
9	as an identity of meromorphic functions. The Euler product defining
10	\(H_f\) is holomorphic in this half-plane. All constants constructed below
11	are independent of the real variable \(H\geq1\).
12	
13	## 1. The external statements used
14	
15	The only external source used is H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan,
16	*Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory* (2007), Chapter 10,
17	pp. 329–330, [doi:10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012),
18	as supplied in
19	`papers/montgomery-vaughan-2007/analytic_properties_of_the_zeta_function_and_lfunctions.pdf`.
20	Here are the two statements used, quoted verbatim, with mathematical
21	typesetting transcribed from the PDF.
22	
23	> **Corollary 10.4** For all \(s\ne1\),
24	> \[
25	> \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin\frac{\pi s}{2}.
26	> \tag{10.9}
27	> \]
28	
29	> **Corollary 10.5** Suppose that \(A>0\) is fixed. Then
30	> \[
31	> |\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|
32	> \]
33	> uniformly for \(|\sigma|\leq A\) and \(|t|\geq1\). Here
34	> \(\tau=|t|+4\), as usual.
35	
36	Both quotations were checked against rendered pages of the supplied PDF.
37	For Corollary 10.4 we will only need \(-5/8\leq\Re s<0\) and a
38	neighborhood of zero. These points satisfy \(s\ne1\). In the negative
39	strip \(\Re(1-s)>1\), so \(\zeta(1-s)\) is analytic there;
40	\(\Gamma(1-s)\) is analytic there because its argument has positive real
41	part. At zero, the pole of \(\zeta(1-s)\) is canceled by
42	\(\sin(\pi s/2)\). Thus \(\zeta(s)\) is analytic in the negative strip
43	and at zero. In the positive half-plane its only pole is the simple pole
44	at one with residue one; this also follows directly from (3) below.
45	
46	For Corollary 10.5 we fix \(A=2\), and use it only when
47	\(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\) and \(|t|\geq2\). Hence \(A>0\),
48	\(|\sigma|\leq A\), and \(|t|\geq1\) all hold throughout its use.
49	Let \(Q>0\) be a constant such that its upper inequality reads
50	\[
51	|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
52	\leq Q(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-\sigma-it)|
53	\tag{2}
54	\]
55	in this range. No conditional estimate for zeta is used.
56	
57	## 2. Bounds throughout the contour strip
58	
59	We first derive a positive-half-plane estimate, including its dependence
60	on the imaginary part. For an integer \(N\geq1\), partial summation of
61	the tail of the defining series gives, initially for \(\Re s>1\),
62	\[
63	\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}
64	       +\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}
65	       -s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du.
66	\tag{3}
67	\]
68	Indeed, write the tail as \(\int_N^\infty u^{-s}\,d\lfloor u\rfloor\),
69	replace \(\lfloor u\rfloor\) by \(u-\{u\}\), and integrate the second
70	term by parts. The boundary term at \(N\) vanishes because \(N\) is an
71	integer. The integral in (3) converges locally uniformly for
72	\(\Re s>0\), since \(0\leq\{u\}<1\); hence (3) holds there by analytic
73	continuation, away from \(s=1\). It also shows that the residue at one is
74	one and that there are no other poles in that half-plane.
75	
76	Let \(s=\alpha+iv\), \(V=|v|\geq2\),
77	\(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6\), and \(\delta\in\{1/4,3/4\}\). Choose
78	\(N=\lceil V\rceil\), so \(V\leq N\leq3V/2\). The finite sum in (3)
79	has exactly \(N\) terms. Each term has modulus at most \(n^{-\delta}\),
80	and after summation its modulus is at most
81	\[
82	\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-\delta}
83	\leq1+\int_1^N u^{-\delta}\,du
84	\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}
85	\leq\frac{(3/2)^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}.
86	\]
87	The other two terms satisfy
88	\[
89	\left|\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}\right|
90	\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{V}
91	\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{-\delta}
92	\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}
93	\]
94	and
95	\[
96	\left|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du\right|
97	\leq\frac{|s|}{\alpha}N^{-\alpha}
98	\leq\frac{V+6}{\delta}V^{-\delta}
99	\leq\frac4\delta V^{1-\delta}.
100	\]
101	Consequently, with the explicit constants
102	\[
103	C_\delta=(3/2)^{1-\delta}
104	              \left(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\right)+\frac4\delta,
105	\]
106	we have
107	\[
108	|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\leq C_\delta V^{1-\delta}
109	\quad(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6,\ V\geq2).
110	\tag{4}
111	\]
112	
113	Now put \(s=\sigma+it\), \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2\), and \(T=|t|\geq2\).
114	For \(1/4\leq\sigma\leq2\), (4) with \(\delta=1/4\) gives
115	\[
116	|\zeta(s)|\leq C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\leq C_{1/4}T^{11/8}.
117	\]
118	For \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\), the real part of \(1-s\) lies in
119	\([3/4,13/8]\), so (4) with \(\delta=3/4\), followed by (2), gives
120	\[
121	\begin{aligned}
122	|\zeta(s)|
123	&\leq Q(T+4)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\\
124	&\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{3/4-\sigma}
125	\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}.
126	\end{aligned}
127	\]
128	Here \(T+4\leq3T\) and \(1/4\leq1/2-\sigma\leq9/8\).
129	Also \(3/4\leq\Re(2s+2)\leq6\), and its imaginary part has modulus
130	\(2T\geq4\). Thus
131	\[
132	|\zeta(2s+2)|\leq C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4}.
133	\tag{5}
134	\]
135	
136	We next obtain a bound for \(H_f(s)\) uniform on this whole strip.
137	This is a uniformity supplement to the fixed-line bound in P5; we do not
138	need to strengthen its domain of continuation. Write \(d=\deg f\), and
139	let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite set of primes dividing every coefficient
140	of \(f\). For \(p\notin\mathcal B\), its reduction is a nonzero
141	polynomial over \(\mathbb F_p\), with at most \(d\) roots. Each residue
142	modulo \(p\) has exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\), whence
143	\[
144	0\leq\rho(p)\leq d,\qquad0\leq\rho(p^2)\leq dp.
145	\tag{6}
146	\]
147	Use the quantities \(a_p,b_p,c_p\) defined in P5, and put
148	\(u_p=b_p-a_p\), \(q_p=c_p-b_p\). Since \(p^2-2\geq p^2/2\), (6)
149	gives
150	\[
151	\begin{gathered}
152	|a_p-1|\leq2dp^{-3},\qquad |u_p|\leq4dp^{-3},
153	\qquad |q_p|\leq(d+2)p^{-2},\\
154	|q_p-p^{-2}|\leq(2+2d)p^{-3},
155	\qquad |q_p-a_pp^{-2}|\leq(2+4d)p^{-3},\\
156	|(1-2p^{-2})a_p-1|\leq(2+4d)p^{-2}.
157	\end{gathered}
158	\tag{7}
159	\]
160	For the fourth inequality, the exact difference is
161	\[
162	q_p-p^{-2}=\frac{2-p\rho(p)}{p^2(p^2-2)},
163	\]
164	whose modulus is at most \(4p^{-4}+2dp^{-3}\leq(2+2d)p^{-3}\).
165	The fifth follows by adding \(|a_p-1|p^{-2}\leq2dp^{-5}\).
166	For the last inequality, the bound before collecting powers is
167	\(2dp^{-3}+2p^{-2}+4dp^{-5}\), which is at most the stated bound.
168	
169	Set \(z=p^{-s}\). The local factor of \(H_f\) is exactly
170	\[
171	L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})
172	 \left[a_p+u_pz+(q_p-a_pp^{-2})z^2
173	                    -u_pp^{-2}z^3-q_pp^{-2}z^4\right].
174	\]
175	Since \(|z|=p^{-\sigma}\leq p^{5/8}\), (7) implies
176	\[
177	\begin{aligned}
178	|L_p(s)-1|\leq{}& (2+4d)p^{-2}+4dp^{-19/8}
179	 +(2+4d)p^{-7/4}\\
180	&+4dp^{-25/8}+(d+2)p^{-3/2}
181	\leq(6+17d)p^{-3/2}.
182	\end{aligned}
183	\tag{8}
184	\]
185	The prime sum of these bounds is at most
186	\[
187	(6+17d)\sum_{n=2}^\infty n^{-3/2}
188	\leq(6+17d)\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du
189	=2(6+17d).
190	\]
191	Thus the product over \(p\notin\mathcal B\) has modulus at most
192	\(\exp(2(6+17d))\). The remaining product has exactly
193	\(|\mathcal B|\) factors. Before multiplication each such factor is
194	bounded by the following finite number:
195	\[
196	U_p=(1-2p^{-2})(1+p^{-3/4})
197	       \left(|a_p|+|u_p|p^{5/8}+|q_p|p^{5/4}\right).
198	\]
199	After multiplication their modulus is at most
200	\(\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p\), with the empty product equal to one.
201	Therefore
202	\[
203	|H_f(s)|\leq M_H,
204	\qquad
205	M_H=\exp(2(6+17d))\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p,
206	\quad -5/8\leq\Re s\leq2.
207	\tag{9}
208	\]
209	Combining (1), (4), (5), and (9), define
210	\[
211	C_D=M_H\max\{C_{1/4},Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}\}
212	                    2^{1/4}C_{3/4}.
213	\]
214	We then have the explicit growth estimate
215	\[
216	|D_f(\sigma+it)|\leq C_D|t|^{13/8}
217	\quad(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2,\ |t|\geq2),
218	\tag{10}
219	\]
220	where the exponent is \(11/8+1/4=13/8\).
221	
222	## 3. Mellin representation and contour displacement
223	
224	The elementary kernel identity needed here is, for \(v>0\),
225	\[
226	\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}
227	             \frac{2v^z}{z(z+1)(z+2)}\,dz
228	=\begin{cases}(1-v^{-1})^2,&v\geq1,\\0,&0<v<1.\end{cases}
229	\tag{11}
230	\]
231	For completeness, close a finite rectangle to the left when \(v\geq1\),
232	and to the right when \(v<1\). On a fixed horizontal segment at height
233	\(T\), the denominator has modulus at least \(T^3\), so those integrals
234	tend to zero as \(T\) tends to infinity. A new left edge
235	\(\Re z=-N-1/2\), \(N\geq3\), has normalized integral in modulus at most
236	\[
237	\frac{v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi}
238	\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
239	       \frac{dt}{((N-3/2)^2+t^2)^{3/2}}
240	=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2},
241	\]
242	because each of
243	\(|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|\) is at least
244	\(\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\Im z)^2}\). This tends to zero also at \(v=1\).
245	A new right edge \(\Re z=N\) has normalized integral at most
246	\(2v^N/(\pi N^2)\), which tends to zero for \(v<1\). The left-hand residues
247	are \(1,-2v^{-1},v^{-2}\), respectively, at \(0,-1,-2\). Their sum is
248	the first expression in (11), including its value zero at \(v=1\).
249	
250	Apply (11) with \(v=H/h\), multiply by \(H^2W_f(h)/h\), and sum over
251	positive integers \(h\). P5 gives
252	\(A_2:=\sum_{h=1}^\infty|W_f(h)|h^{-2}<\infty\).
253	On putting \(s=z+1\), the sum of absolute values of the integrands on
254	\(\Re s=2\) is bounded by
255	\[
256	\frac{2H^3 A_2}{|(s-1)s(s+1)|}.
257	\]
258	Its integral over the entire vertical line is finite: for \(|\Im s|\geq1\)
259	it is at most \(2H^3A_2|\Im s|^{-3}\), and on the remaining compact
260	segment the denominator does not vanish. Absolute convergence therefore
261	justifies the exchange of the infinite sum and integral. It gives
262	\[
263	\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\,ds,
264	\qquad
265	G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
266	\tag{12}
267	\]
268	The equality holds for all real \(H\geq1\); an integer endpoint has
269	weight zero in both (11) and the definition of \(\Theta_f\).
270	
271	Shift the contour to \(\Re s=-5/8\). The only possible poles of
272	\(D_f\) in the intervening strip are at \(1\) and \(-1/2\), from
273	\(\zeta(s)\) and \(\zeta(2s+2)\), respectively. This follows from
274	(1), the analyticity of \(H_f\) supplied by P5, and the zeta properties
275	checked in Section 1. The kernel additionally has a pole at zero; its
276	pole at \(-1\) lies outside the strip.
277	
278	Here are explicit bounds justifying the displacement. At heights
279	\(\pm T\), \(T\geq2\), each denominator factor in (12) has modulus at
280	least \(T\), while \(H^{\sigma+1}\leq H^3\) because \(H\geq1\).
281	Thus (10) gives the bound
282	\[
283	|G_H(\sigma\pm iT)|\leq2C_DH^3T^{13/8-3}
284	                         =2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}.
285	\]
286	Each horizontal segment has length \(2+5/8=21/8\). After integration
287	over both segments, the bound is at most
288	\[
289	\frac{21}{2}C_DH^3T^{-11/8},
290	\]
291	which tends to zero for each fixed \(H\). This limit is taken before
292	asserting the uniform bound for the resulting left vertical integral.
293	
294	For that vertical line define the finite constant
295	\[
296	M_0=\max_{|t|\leq2}|D_f(-5/8+it)|.
297	\]
298	It is finite because the line contains no poles. Its denominator in
299	(12) satisfies, for all real \(t\),
300	\[
301	|(s-1)s(s+1)|\geq\frac{13}{8}\frac58\frac38=\frac{195}{512}.
302	\]
303	The compact part of the line has length four; before integration its
304	integrand is bounded by
305	\((1024/195)M_0H^{3/8}\), so after integration it contributes at most
306	\((4096/195)M_0H^{3/8}\) to the absolute integral. On either infinite
307	tail, (10) gives
308	\[
309	|G_H(-5/8+it)|\leq2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}
310	\qquad(|t|\geq2).
311	\]
312	After integration over both tails the bound is
313	\[
314	4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\,dt
315	=\frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}.
316	\]
317	In particular, the left integral is absolutely convergent, and
318	\[
319	\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-5/8-i\infty}^{-5/8+i\infty}
320	                                      G_H(s)\,ds\right|
321	\leq C_*H^{3/8},
322	\tag{13}
323	\]
324	where the finite constant depending only on \(f\) can be taken to be
325	\[
326	C_* =\frac1{2\pi}
327	       \left(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+
328	                         \frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}\right).
329	\tag{14}
330	\]
331	The residue theorem on the finite rectangles, followed by the limits
332	just justified, now gives (12) as the sum of the three residues and the
333	left integral.
334	
335	## 4. Residues and the two estimates
336	
337	Write the Laurent expansion at one as
338	\[
339	D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+(s-1)J_f(s),
340	\]
341	Here P5 identifies \(R_f=P_f(1)\), and the definition in the statement
342	gives \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\). Here \(J_f\) is analytic on a fixed disk
343	about one. On a smaller closed disk choose a finite constant \(A_f\)
344	with \(|J_f(s)|\leq A_f\); the local remainder is therefore bounded
345	by \(A_f|s-1|\). No such
346	local remainder is summed or integrated in the argument.
347	
348	Set \(q(s)=2/[s(s+1)]\). Direct differentiation gives
349	\(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). Hence the residue of
350	\(q(s)D_f(s)H^{s+1}/(s-1)\) at one is exactly
351	\[
352	H^2\left(L_f+R_f\log H-\frac32R_f\right)
353	=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
354	\tag{15}
355	\]
356	At zero, P5 gives \(D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))=-c/2\), and consequently
357	\[
358	\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=0}G_H(s)
359	=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
360	\tag{16}
361	\]
362	At \(-1/2\), the denominator \((s-1)s(s+1)\) equals \(3/8\).
363	Using exactly the definition of \(K_f\) in the statement, we obtain
364	\[
365	\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}G_H(s)
366	=\frac{16}{3}H^{1/2}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
367	=-K_fH^{1/2}.
368	\tag{17}
369	\]
370	This definition agrees with the one in P5: the simple pole of
371	\(\zeta(2s+2)\) has residue \(1/2\), so (1) gives
372	\[
373	-\frac{16}{3}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
374	=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2).
375	\]
376	
377	Let \(E_f(H)\) denote the normalized left vertical integral in (13).
378	Equations (12)–(17) establish the exact formula
379	\[
380	\Theta_f(H)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}+E_f(H),
381	\qquad |E_f(H)|\leq C_*H^{3/8}
382	\tag{18}
383	\]
384	for every real \(H\geq1\). Thus no loss depending on whether \(H\) is
385	an integer is present. Choose \(C(f)=1+C_*\), which is strictly positive.
386	The first asserted inequality follows from (18). Substituting (18) into
387	the definition of \(F_f\) gives the exact identity
388	\[
389	F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-\frac{E_f(H)}{H^2}.
390	\]
391	Therefore
392	\[
393	|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|
394	\leq C_*H^{3/8-2}=C_*H^{-13/8}
395	\leq C(f)H^{-13/8},
396	\]
397	which proves the second assertion with the same constant.
398	
399	## 5. The integral identity
400	
401	Fix real \(x\geq2\) and \(2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x\), and put
402	\(r_+=\max(r,0)\). Throughout \(Z\leq t\leq Y\), every nonzero
403	term of the integrand has \(h\leq x/Z\). Thus only
404	\(\lfloor x/Z\rfloor\) integers can occur, and we may write the
405	finite sum identity
406	\[
407	2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
408	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}W_f(h)
409	                                  2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt.
410	\tag{19}
411	\]
412	For each such positive integer \(h\), the function
413	\((x-ht)_+^2\) is continuously differentiable, including at
414	\(t=x/h\), and its derivative is \(-2h(x-ht)_+\). Therefore its
415	integral is exactly
416	\[
417	2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt
418	=\frac{(x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2}{h}.
419	\tag{20}
420	\]
421	Multiplying out the definition of \(\Theta_f\) gives
422	\[
423	Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)
424	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hZ)_+^2,
425	\]
426	and
427	\[
428	Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)
429	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hY)_+^2.
430	\]
431	In the second equality, terms with \(h>x/Y\) vanish, so the indicated
432	extension of its finite summation range changes its value by exactly
433	zero. Subtract these two equalities and use (19)–(20). The result is
434	\[
435	2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
436	=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
437	\]
438	This is exact throughout the requested range, and has no error term.
439	
440	Exact symbolic checks in Python/SymPy verified the local-factor
441	expansion, the kernel coefficient at \(-1/2\), the kernel residue at
442	zero, and \(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). No numerical sanity check was
443	used. No excluded source or previous-run write-up was consulted, and no
444	objections file was supplied for this attempt.

# Proof of P6

We use P5 as a black box, with the notation in `statement.md` and
`deps/P5.md`. In particular,
\[
D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\qquad(\Re s>-3/4),
\tag{1}
\]
as an identity of meromorphic functions. The Euler product defining
\(H_f\) is holomorphic in this half-plane. All constants constructed below
are independent of the real variable \(H\geq1\).

## 1. The external statements used

The only external source used is H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan,
*Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory* (2007), Chapter 10,
pp. 329–330, [doi:10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012),
as supplied in
`papers/montgomery-vaughan-2007/analytic_properties_of_the_zeta_function_and_lfunctions.pdf`.
Here are the two statements used, quoted verbatim, with mathematical
typesetting transcribed from the PDF.

> **Corollary 10.4** For all \(s\ne1\),
> \[
> \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin\frac{\pi s}{2}.
> \tag{10.9}
> \]

> **Corollary 10.5** Suppose that \(A>0\) is fixed. Then
> \[
> |\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|
> \]
> uniformly for \(|\sigma|\leq A\) and \(|t|\geq1\). Here
> \(\tau=|t|+4\), as usual.

Both quotations were checked against rendered pages of the supplied PDF.
For Corollary 10.4 we will only need \(-5/8\leq\Re s<0\) and a
neighborhood of zero. These points satisfy \(s\ne1\). In the negative
strip \(\Re(1-s)>1\), so \(\zeta(1-s)\) is analytic there;
\(\Gamma(1-s)\) is analytic there because its argument has positive real
part. At zero, the pole of \(\zeta(1-s)\) is canceled by
\(\sin(\pi s/2)\). Thus \(\zeta(s)\) is analytic in the negative strip
and at zero. In the positive half-plane its only pole is the simple pole
at one with residue one; this also follows directly from (3) below.

For Corollary 10.5 we fix \(A=2\), and use it only when
\(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\) and \(|t|\geq2\). Hence \(A>0\),
\(|\sigma|\leq A\), and \(|t|\geq1\) all hold throughout its use.
Let \(Q>0\) be a constant such that its upper inequality reads
\[
|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
\leq Q(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-\sigma-it)|
\tag{2}
\]
in this range. No conditional estimate for zeta is used.

## 2. Bounds throughout the contour strip

We first derive a positive-half-plane estimate, including its dependence
on the imaginary part. For an integer \(N\geq1\), partial summation of
the tail of the defining series gives, initially for \(\Re s>1\),
\[
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}
       +\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}
       -s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, write the tail as \(\int_N^\infty u^{-s}\,d\lfloor u\rfloor\),
replace \(\lfloor u\rfloor\) by \(u-\{u\}\), and integrate the second
term by parts. The boundary term at \(N\) vanishes because \(N\) is an
integer. The integral in (3) converges locally uniformly for
\(\Re s>0\), since \(0\leq\{u\}<1\); hence (3) holds there by analytic
continuation, away from \(s=1\). It also shows that the residue at one is
one and that there are no other poles in that half-plane.

Let \(s=\alpha+iv\), \(V=|v|\geq2\),
\(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6\), and \(\delta\in\{1/4,3/4\}\). Choose
\(N=\lceil V\rceil\), so \(V\leq N\leq3V/2\). The finite sum in (3)
has exactly \(N\) terms. Each term has modulus at most \(n^{-\delta}\),
and after summation its modulus is at most
\[
\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-\delta}
\leq1+\int_1^N u^{-\delta}\,du
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}
\leq\frac{(3/2)^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}.
\]
The other two terms satisfy
\[
\left|\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}\right|
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{V}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}
\]
and
\[
\left|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du\right|
\leq\frac{|s|}{\alpha}N^{-\alpha}
\leq\frac{V+6}{\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq\frac4\delta V^{1-\delta}.
\]
Consequently, with the explicit constants
\[
C_\delta=(3/2)^{1-\delta}
              \left(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\right)+\frac4\delta,
\]
we have
\[
|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\leq C_\delta V^{1-\delta}
\quad(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6,\ V\geq2).
\tag{4}
\]

Now put \(s=\sigma+it\), \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2\), and \(T=|t|\geq2\).
For \(1/4\leq\sigma\leq2\), (4) with \(\delta=1/4\) gives
\[
|\zeta(s)|\leq C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\leq C_{1/4}T^{11/8}.
\]
For \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\), the real part of \(1-s\) lies in
\([3/4,13/8]\), so (4) with \(\delta=3/4\), followed by (2), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\zeta(s)|
&\leq Q(T+4)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\\
&\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{3/4-\sigma}
\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(T+4\leq3T\) and \(1/4\leq1/2-\sigma\leq9/8\).
Also \(3/4\leq\Re(2s+2)\leq6\), and its imaginary part has modulus
\(2T\geq4\). Thus
\[
|\zeta(2s+2)|\leq C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4}.
\tag{5}
\]

We next obtain a bound for \(H_f(s)\) uniform on this whole strip.
This is a uniformity supplement to the fixed-line bound in P5; we do not
need to strengthen its domain of continuation. Write \(d=\deg f\), and
let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite set of primes dividing every coefficient
of \(f\). For \(p\notin\mathcal B\), its reduction is a nonzero
polynomial over \(\mathbb F_p\), with at most \(d\) roots. Each residue
modulo \(p\) has exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\), whence
\[
0\leq\rho(p)\leq d,\qquad0\leq\rho(p^2)\leq dp.
\tag{6}
\]
Use the quantities \(a_p,b_p,c_p\) defined in P5, and put
\(u_p=b_p-a_p\), \(q_p=c_p-b_p\). Since \(p^2-2\geq p^2/2\), (6)
gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
|a_p-1|\leq2dp^{-3},\qquad |u_p|\leq4dp^{-3},
\qquad |q_p|\leq(d+2)p^{-2},\\
|q_p-p^{-2}|\leq(2+2d)p^{-3},
\qquad |q_p-a_pp^{-2}|\leq(2+4d)p^{-3},\\
|(1-2p^{-2})a_p-1|\leq(2+4d)p^{-2}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{7}
\]
For the fourth inequality, the exact difference is
\[
q_p-p^{-2}=\frac{2-p\rho(p)}{p^2(p^2-2)},
\]
whose modulus is at most \(4p^{-4}+2dp^{-3}\leq(2+2d)p^{-3}\).
The fifth follows by adding \(|a_p-1|p^{-2}\leq2dp^{-5}\).
For the last inequality, the bound before collecting powers is
\(2dp^{-3}+2p^{-2}+4dp^{-5}\), which is at most the stated bound.

Set \(z=p^{-s}\). The local factor of \(H_f\) is exactly
\[
L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})
 \left[a_p+u_pz+(q_p-a_pp^{-2})z^2
                    -u_pp^{-2}z^3-q_pp^{-2}z^4\right].
\]
Since \(|z|=p^{-\sigma}\leq p^{5/8}\), (7) implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
|L_p(s)-1|\leq{}& (2+4d)p^{-2}+4dp^{-19/8}
 +(2+4d)p^{-7/4}\\
&+4dp^{-25/8}+(d+2)p^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)p^{-3/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
The prime sum of these bounds is at most
\[
(6+17d)\sum_{n=2}^\infty n^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du
=2(6+17d).
\]
Thus the product over \(p\notin\mathcal B\) has modulus at most
\(\exp(2(6+17d))\). The remaining product has exactly
\(|\mathcal B|\) factors. Before multiplication each such factor is
bounded by the following finite number:
\[
U_p=(1-2p^{-2})(1+p^{-3/4})
       \left(|a_p|+|u_p|p^{5/8}+|q_p|p^{5/4}\right).
\]
After multiplication their modulus is at most
\(\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p\), with the empty product equal to one.
Therefore
\[
|H_f(s)|\leq M_H,
\qquad
M_H=\exp(2(6+17d))\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p,
\quad -5/8\leq\Re s\leq2.
\tag{9}
\]
Combining (1), (4), (5), and (9), define
\[
C_D=M_H\max\{C_{1/4},Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}\}
                    2^{1/4}C_{3/4}.
\]
We then have the explicit growth estimate
\[
|D_f(\sigma+it)|\leq C_D|t|^{13/8}
\quad(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2,\ |t|\geq2),
\tag{10}
\]
where the exponent is \(11/8+1/4=13/8\).

## 3. Mellin representation and contour displacement

The elementary kernel identity needed here is, for \(v>0\),
\[
\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}
             \frac{2v^z}{z(z+1)(z+2)}\,dz
=\begin{cases}(1-v^{-1})^2,&v\geq1,\\0,&0<v<1.\end{cases}
\tag{11}
\]
For completeness, close a finite rectangle to the left when \(v\geq1\),
and to the right when \(v<1\). On a fixed horizontal segment at height
\(T\), the denominator has modulus at least \(T^3\), so those integrals
tend to zero as \(T\) tends to infinity. A new left edge
\(\Re z=-N-1/2\), \(N\geq3\), has normalized integral in modulus at most
\[
\frac{v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
       \frac{dt}{((N-3/2)^2+t^2)^{3/2}}
=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2},
\]
because each of
\(|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|\) is at least
\(\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\Im z)^2}\). This tends to zero also at \(v=1\).
A new right edge \(\Re z=N\) has normalized integral at most
\(2v^N/(\pi N^2)\), which tends to zero for \(v<1\). The left-hand residues
are \(1,-2v^{-1},v^{-2}\), respectively, at \(0,-1,-2\). Their sum is
the first expression in (11), including its value zero at \(v=1\).

Apply (11) with \(v=H/h\), multiply by \(H^2W_f(h)/h\), and sum over
positive integers \(h\). P5 gives
\(A_2:=\sum_{h=1}^\infty|W_f(h)|h^{-2}<\infty\).
On putting \(s=z+1\), the sum of absolute values of the integrands on
\(\Re s=2\) is bounded by
\[
\frac{2H^3 A_2}{|(s-1)s(s+1)|}.
\]
Its integral over the entire vertical line is finite: for \(|\Im s|\geq1\)
it is at most \(2H^3A_2|\Im s|^{-3}\), and on the remaining compact
segment the denominator does not vanish. Absolute convergence therefore
justifies the exchange of the infinite sum and integral. It gives
\[
\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\,ds,
\qquad
G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
\tag{12}
\]
The equality holds for all real \(H\geq1\); an integer endpoint has
weight zero in both (11) and the definition of \(\Theta_f\).

Shift the contour to \(\Re s=-5/8\). The only possible poles of
\(D_f\) in the intervening strip are at \(1\) and \(-1/2\), from
\(\zeta(s)\) and \(\zeta(2s+2)\), respectively. This follows from
(1), the analyticity of \(H_f\) supplied by P5, and the zeta properties
checked in Section 1. The kernel additionally has a pole at zero; its
pole at \(-1\) lies outside the strip.

Here are explicit bounds justifying the displacement. At heights
\(\pm T\), \(T\geq2\), each denominator factor in (12) has modulus at
least \(T\), while \(H^{\sigma+1}\leq H^3\) because \(H\geq1\).
Thus (10) gives the bound
\[
|G_H(\sigma\pm iT)|\leq2C_DH^3T^{13/8-3}
                         =2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}.
\]
Each horizontal segment has length \(2+5/8=21/8\). After integration
over both segments, the bound is at most
\[
\frac{21}{2}C_DH^3T^{-11/8},
\]
which tends to zero for each fixed \(H\). This limit is taken before
asserting the uniform bound for the resulting left vertical integral.

For that vertical line define the finite constant
\[
M_0=\max_{|t|\leq2}|D_f(-5/8+it)|.
\]
It is finite because the line contains no poles. Its denominator in
(12) satisfies, for all real \(t\),
\[
|(s-1)s(s+1)|\geq\frac{13}{8}\frac58\frac38=\frac{195}{512}.
\]
The compact part of the line has length four; before integration its
integrand is bounded by
\((1024/195)M_0H^{3/8}\), so after integration it contributes at most
\((4096/195)M_0H^{3/8}\) to the absolute integral. On either infinite
tail, (10) gives
\[
|G_H(-5/8+it)|\leq2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}
\qquad(|t|\geq2).
\]
After integration over both tails the bound is
\[
4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\,dt
=\frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}.
\]
In particular, the left integral is absolutely convergent, and
\[
\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-5/8-i\infty}^{-5/8+i\infty}
                                      G_H(s)\,ds\right|
\leq C_*H^{3/8},
\tag{13}
\]
where the finite constant depending only on \(f\) can be taken to be
\[
C_* =\frac1{2\pi}
       \left(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+
                         \frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}\right).
\tag{14}
\]
The residue theorem on the finite rectangles, followed by the limits
just justified, now gives (12) as the sum of the three residues and the
left integral.

## 4. Residues and the two estimates

Write the Laurent expansion at one as
\[
D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+(s-1)J_f(s),
\]
Here P5 identifies \(R_f=P_f(1)\), and the definition in the statement
gives \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\). Here \(J_f\) is analytic on a fixed disk
about one. On a smaller closed disk choose a finite constant \(A_f\)
with \(|J_f(s)|\leq A_f\); the local remainder is therefore bounded
by \(A_f|s-1|\). No such
local remainder is summed or integrated in the argument.

Set \(q(s)=2/[s(s+1)]\). Direct differentiation gives
\(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). Hence the residue of
\(q(s)D_f(s)H^{s+1}/(s-1)\) at one is exactly
\[
H^2\left(L_f+R_f\log H-\frac32R_f\right)
=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
\tag{15}
\]
At zero, P5 gives \(D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))=-c/2\), and consequently
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=0}G_H(s)
=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
\tag{16}
\]
At \(-1/2\), the denominator \((s-1)s(s+1)\) equals \(3/8\).
Using exactly the definition of \(K_f\) in the statement, we obtain
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}G_H(s)
=\frac{16}{3}H^{1/2}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-K_fH^{1/2}.
\tag{17}
\]
This definition agrees with the one in P5: the simple pole of
\(\zeta(2s+2)\) has residue \(1/2\), so (1) gives
\[
-\frac{16}{3}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2).
\]

Let \(E_f(H)\) denote the normalized left vertical integral in (13).
Equations (12)–(17) establish the exact formula
\[
\Theta_f(H)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}+E_f(H),
\qquad |E_f(H)|\leq C_*H^{3/8}
\tag{18}
\]
for every real \(H\geq1\). Thus no loss depending on whether \(H\) is
an integer is present. Choose \(C(f)=1+C_*\), which is strictly positive.
The first asserted inequality follows from (18). Substituting (18) into
the definition of \(F_f\) gives the exact identity
\[
F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-\frac{E_f(H)}{H^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|
\leq C_*H^{3/8-2}=C_*H^{-13/8}
\leq C(f)H^{-13/8},
\]
which proves the second assertion with the same constant.

## 5. The integral identity

Fix real \(x\geq2\) and \(2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x\), and put
\(r_+=\max(r,0)\). Throughout \(Z\leq t\leq Y\), every nonzero
term of the integrand has \(h\leq x/Z\). Thus only
\(\lfloor x/Z\rfloor\) integers can occur, and we may write the
finite sum identity
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}W_f(h)
                                  2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt.
\tag{19}
\]
For each such positive integer \(h\), the function
\((x-ht)_+^2\) is continuously differentiable, including at
\(t=x/h\), and its derivative is \(-2h(x-ht)_+\). Therefore its
integral is exactly
\[
2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt
=\frac{(x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2}{h}.
\tag{20}
\]
Multiplying out the definition of \(\Theta_f\) gives
\[
Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hZ)_+^2,
\]
and
\[
Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hY)_+^2.
\]
In the second equality, terms with \(h>x/Y\) vanish, so the indicated
extension of its finite summation range changes its value by exactly
zero. Subtract these two equalities and use (19)–(20). The result is
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\]
This is exact throughout the requested range, and has no error term.

Exact symbolic checks in Python/SymPy verified the local-factor
expansion, the kernel coefficient at \(-1/2\), the kernel residue at
zero, and \(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). No numerical sanity check was
used. No excluded source or previous-run write-up was consulted, and no
objections file was supplied for this attempt.

4	\]
5	For every prime \(p\nmid A_d\), reduction modulo \(p\) is a nonzero
6	polynomial of degree \(d\), so the factor theorem gives at most \(d\)
7	roots. If \(p\mid A_d\), the bound
8	\(\rho(p)\le p\le |A_d|\) applies. Each residue class modulo \(p\) has
9	exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\). Consequently,
10	\[
11	0\le\rho(p)\le\min\{C_0,p\},\qquad
12	0\le\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)\le C_0p.                 \tag{1}
13	\]
14	These bounds require no assumption on the content, discriminant, or
15	factorization of \(f\).
16	
17	We will use the following explicit summation estimate. If \(u>1\) and
18	\(N\ge1\) is an integer, comparison with an integral gives
19	\[
20	\sum_{p>N}p^{-u}\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-u}
21	\le\int_N^\infty t^{-u}\,dt
22	=\frac{N^{1-u}}{u-1}.                              \tag{2}
23	\]
24	Both sums in (2) have infinitely many possible indices. A bound
25	\(k p^{-u}\) for each prime therefore has total at most
26	\(kN^{1-u}/(u-1)\) after summing over \(p>N\). In particular, the sum over
27	all primes is at most \(k/(u-1)\).
28	If local factors are \(1+e_p(s)\), the estimate
29	\[
30	\left|\prod_{p>N}(1+e_p(s))-1\right|
31	\le \exp\!\left(\sum_{p>N}|e_p(s)|\right)-1          \tag{3}
32	\]
33	follows first for finite products by expansion and then for their limits.
34	Thus all the prime-sum tail estimates below also give explicit product
35	tail estimates. Uniform summability of \(|e_p|\) on compact sets gives
36	local uniform convergence to a holomorphic function, since the finite
37	products are holomorphic.
38	
39	For brevity put \(q_p=1-2/p^2\), and introduce the three coefficients
40	\[
41	\begin{aligned}
42	\alpha_p&=q_pa_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
43	\beta_p&=q_p(b_p-a_p)=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}
44	                              -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
45	\delta_p&=q_p(c_p-b_p)=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
46	\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
47	\]
48	By (1),
49	\[
50	\begin{gathered}
51	0<q_p\le\alpha_p\le1,\qquad
52	0\le\beta_p\le C_0p^{-3},\qquad
53	0\le\delta_p\le p^{-2},\\
54	|\alpha_p-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3},\qquad
55	\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}.                 \tag{5}
56	\end{gathered}
57	\]
58	In particular, \(b_p-a_p\ge0\) and \(c_p-b_p\ge0\).
59	
60	The local factor \(w_p(h)\) in \(W_f(h)\) is, according as
61	\(v_p(h)=0,1\) or at least \(2\),
62	\[
63	w_p(h)=\alpha_p,\quad
64	\alpha_p+\beta_p,\quad
65	\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p,
66	\]
67	respectively. Alternatively, the elementary bound
68	\(0\le\rho(p^j)\le p^j\), including \(j=0\), gives directly
69	\[
70	1-\frac2{p^2}\le w_p(h)\le1-\frac1{p^2},\qquad
71	|w_p(h)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}.                          \tag{6}
72	\]
73	The prime tail of the last bound is at most \(2/N\) by (2), uniformly
74	in \(h\). Every factor is at least \(1/2\). For \(1/2\le t\le1\),
75	\(-\log t\le2(1-t)\); hence
76	\[
77	\sum_p|\log w_p(h)|\le4\sum_pp^{-2}\le4.
78	\]
79	It follows that the product defining \(W_f(h)\) is absolutely convergent
80	and \(0<W_f(h)\le1\). For \(s=\sigma+it\) with \(\sigma>1\), this gives
81	\[
82	\sum_{h\ge1}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_{h\ge1}h^{-\sigma}<\infty.
83	\]
84	More explicitly, the sum of the errors over the infinitely many indices
85	\(h>N\) is bounded by
86	\[
87	\sum_{h>N}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|
88	\le\sum_{h>N}h^{-\sigma}
89	\le\frac{N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                  \tag{7}
90	\]
91	This proves the asserted absolute convergence of \(D_f\).
92	
93	Write
94	\[
95	L_p(s)=q_pB_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s}.
96	\]
97	On the closed half-plane \(\Re s\ge\sigma\), (5) gives the bound for
98	each individual prime
99	\[
100	|L_p(s)-1|
101	\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}.       \tag{8}
102	\]
103	If \(\sigma>-1/2\), all four exponents exceed \(1\). Summing (8) over
104	the infinitely many primes \(p>N\), using (2) separately for its four
105	terms, yields
106	\[
107	\begin{aligned}
108	\sum_{p>N}|L_p(s)-1|\le E_P(N;\sigma)
109	={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
110	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
111	 +\frac{N^{-1-2\sigma}}{1+2\sigma}.                 \tag{9}
112	\end{aligned}
113	\]
114	Every power of \(N\) on the right has negative exponent. Equations
115	(3) and (9) prove absolute and locally uniform convergence of \(P_f\)
116	on \(\Re s>-1/2\). They also prove its holomorphy there.
117	
118	The local factor in \(H_f\) is
119	\[
120	\begin{aligned}
121	M_p(s)&=(1-p^{-2s-2})L_p(s)\\
122	 &=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}
123	 +(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2})p^{-2s}
124	 -\beta_pp^{-2}p^{-3s}-\delta_pp^{-2}p^{-4s}.         \tag{10}
125	\end{aligned}
126	\]
127	The coefficient where cancellation is needed is exactly
128	\[
129	\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}
130	 =-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}
131	                         -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6},
132	\]
133	so its absolute value is at most
134	\(C_0p^{-3}+2p^{-4}+C_0p^{-5}\). Thus, for \(\Re s\ge\sigma\),
135	\[
136	\begin{aligned}
137	|M_p(s)-1|\le{}&2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}
138	 +C_0p^{-3-2\sigma}+2p^{-4-2\sigma}\\
139	 &+C_0p^{-5-2\sigma}+C_0p^{-5-3\sigma}
140	 +p^{-4-4\sigma}.                                  \tag{11}
141	\end{aligned}
142	\]
143	For \(\sigma>-3/4\), the eight exponents on the right are, respectively,
144	\[
145	2,\ 3,\ 3+\sigma,\ 3+2\sigma,\ 4+2\sigma,
146	\ 5+2\sigma,\ 5+3\sigma,\ 4+4\sigma,
147	\]
148	and each is greater than \(1\). The sum over the infinitely many primes
149	\(p>N\), before summation bounded prime by prime by (11), is after
150	summation bounded by
151	\[
152	\begin{aligned}
153	\sum_{p>N}|M_p(s)-1|\le E_H(N;\sigma)
154	={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
155	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
156	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-2\sigma}}{2+2\sigma}\\
157	 &+\frac{2N^{-3-2\sigma}}{3+2\sigma}
158	 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-2\sigma}}{4+2\sigma}
159	 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-3\sigma}}{4+3\sigma}
160	 +\frac{N^{-3-4\sigma}}{3+4\sigma}.                 \tag{12}
161	\end{aligned}
162	\]
163	All denominators in (12) are positive, and all powers of \(N\) have
164	negative exponents in this range. Equations (3) and (12) prove absolute
165	and locally uniform convergence, and holomorphy, of \(H_f\) on
166	\(\Re s>-3/4\). For every real \(t\), the bound
167	\(|M_p(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(|M_p(\sigma+it)-1|)\) also proves
168	\[
169	|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le \exp(E_H(1;\sigma)).             \tag{13}
170	\]
171	Thus one may take \(C(f,\sigma)=\exp(E_H(1;\sigma))\), with every
172	term in its exponent specified in (12).
173	
174	We next identify the Dirichlet series. The positive number
175	\[
176	A=\prod_p\alpha_p
177	\]
178	exists by (5), or by (6) with \(h=1\). Define
179	\(u(h)=W_f(h)/A\). Only the primes dividing \(h\) change a factor of
180	this quotient, so \(u\) is multiplicative and
181	\[
182	u(1)=1,\qquad u(p)=\frac{b_p}{a_p},\qquad
183	u(p^e)=\frac{c_p}{a_p}\quad(e\ge2).
184	\]
185	In particular \(0<u(h)\le A^{-1}\). For \(\Re s>1\), its local series is
186	\[
187	\sum_{e\ge0}u(p^e)p^{-es}
188	 =1+\frac{b_p}{a_p}p^{-s}
189	       +\frac{c_p}{a_p}\frac{p^{-2s}}{1-p^{-s}}
190	 =\frac{B_p(s)}{a_p(1-p^{-s})}.                    \tag{14}
191	\]
192	To justify multiplication of these series, first include only primes
193	\(p\le N\). Their finite product expands into the sum over integers
194	whose prime factors are all at most \(N\). Every omitted integer is
195	greater than \(N\). The omitted sum has infinitely many possible
196	indices, each term has modulus at most \(A^{-1}h^{-\sigma}\), and its
197	total modulus is at most
198	\[
199	\frac{A^{-1}N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                \tag{15}
200	\]
201	This tends to zero. Multiplying (14) over all primes therefore gives
202	\[
203	\begin{aligned}
204	D_f(s)
205	 &=\lim_{N\to\infty}
206	 \left(\prod_{p\le N}\frac{L_p(s)}{1-p^{-s}}\right)
207	 \left(\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p\right)\\
208	 &=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad \Re s>1.                 \tag{16}
209	\end{aligned}
210	\]
211	Here the Euler product for \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\) follows
212	by unique prime factorization: its finite-prime expansion omits only
213	integers \(n>N\), whose total absolute contribution is at most
214	\(N^{1-\sigma}/(\sigma-1)\). The extra tail product in (16) tends to
215	\(1\), with explicit bound
216	\[
217	\left|\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p-1\right|
218	 \le \exp\!\left(\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}\right)-1. \tag{17}
219	\]
220	
221	For \(\Re s>-1/2\), the Euler product for \(\zeta(2s+2)\) is
222	absolutely convergent. Its reciprocal product is nonzero, since
223	\(|p^{-2s-2}|<1\) and
224	\(\sum_p|p^{-2s-2}|<\infty\). Multiplying the absolutely convergent
225	products defining \(P_f\) and \(H_f\) gives
226	\[
227	P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\quad(\Re s>-1/2).          \tag{18}
228	\]
229	In particular, (16) proves both required identities on \(\Re s>1\).
230	
231	For completeness, the zeta-function facts needed for continuation and
232	signs can all be derived directly. For \(\Re w>1\), integrating the
233	counting function of the positive integers gives
234	\[
235	\zeta(w)=w\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-w-1}\,dx
236	 =\frac1{w-1}+\frac12
237	       -w\int_1^\infty(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx.     \tag{19}
238	\]
239	Let
240	\(\mathcal B_2(x)=\{x\}^2-\{x\}+1/6\).
241	This function is continuous at integers, is bounded in absolute value
242	by \(1/6\), and has derivative \(2(\{x\}-1/2)\) between consecutive
243	integers. More explicitly, for an integer \(T\ge2\), integration by
244	parts over the \(T-1\) intervals between \(1\) and \(T\) gives the
245	exact identity
246	\[
247	\int_1^T(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx
248	 =\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}
249	  +\frac{w+1}{2}\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.
250	\]
251	The internal endpoint terms cancel exactly. The upper endpoint
252	term, after multiplication by \(-w\), has modulus
253	\(|w|T^{-\Re w-1}/12\), which tends to zero for \(\Re w>1\).
254	Substitution in (19) therefore yields
255	\[
256	\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}
257	 -\frac{w(w+1)}2
258	       \int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.    \tag{20}
259	\]
260	The integral is holomorphic for \(\Re w>-1\). Explicitly, its tail
261	past \(T\ge1\), including the coefficient in (20), has absolute value
262	at most
263	\[
264	\frac{|w(w+1)|}{12(\Re w+1)}T^{-\Re w-1}.           \tag{21}
265	\]
266	For each nonnegative integer \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the
267	integrand with respect to \(w\) is dominated on \(\Re w\ge\eta>-1\)
268	by \((\log x)^m x^{-\eta-2}/6\), whose integral is
269	\(m!/[6(\eta+1)^{m+1}]\). These bounds justify holomorphy and the
270	continuation in (20), with its sole pole at \(w=1\) and residue \(1\).
271	
272	We also record the constant term at that pole. For an integer \(N\ge1\),
273	the same counting-function integration gives, initially for
274	\(\Re w>1\) and then by continuation for \(\Re w>0\),
275	\[
276	\zeta(w)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}
277	       -w\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-w-1}\,dx.           \tag{22}
278	\]
279	The finite sum has exactly \(N\) terms. The final integral, including
280	its coefficient, is bounded by
281	\(|w|N^{-\Re w}/\Re w\). Subtracting \(1/(w-1)\) and taking
282	\(w\to1\) gives
283	\[
284	\lim_{w\to1}\left(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\right)
285	 =\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n-\log N
286	       -\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-2}\,dx.
287	\]
288	The integral is between \(0\) and \(1/N\). Taking \(N\to\infty\),
289	the right side is Euler's constant \(\gamma_E\), by its defining
290	harmonic-sum limit.
291	
292	Equation (20) gives \(\zeta(0)=-1/2\). At \(w=-1/2\) it gives
293	\[
294	\zeta(-1/2)=-\frac5{24}
295	       +\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-3/2}\,dx.
296	\]
297	The integral has absolute value at most
298	\((1/6)\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx=1/3\). Hence
299	\[
300	-\frac14\le\zeta(-1/2)\le-\frac16<0.              \tag{23}
301	\]
302	
303	For \(\Re s>-3/4\), the two arguments \(s\) and \(2s+2\) in
304	\[
305	\widetilde D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)         \tag{24}
306	\]
307	satisfy \(\Re s>-1\) and \(\Re(2s+2)>1/2>-1\).
308	Thus (20) and the holomorphy of \(H_f\) prove that (24) is
309	meromorphic throughout this region. It agrees with \(D_f\) on
310	\(\Re s>1\) by (16) and (18), so it is the claimed continuation.
311	We henceforth use the notation \(D_f\) for this continuation.
312	
313	At \(s=0\),
314	\[
315	L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2},\qquad
316	P_f(0)=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})=\frac1{\zeta(2)}.
317	\]
318	The equality \(D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)\) extends meromorphically to
319	\(\Re s>-1/2\) by (18) and (24). Both factors are regular at zero,
320	so
321	\[
322	D_f(0)=\zeta(0)P_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}.          \tag{25}
323	\]
324	
325	At \(s=1\), \(P_f\) is holomorphic. With \(R_f=P_f(1)\), equations
326	(16) and (22) show
327	\[
328	\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}D_f(s)=R_f,\qquad
329	\lim_{s\to1}\left(D_f(s)-\frac{R_f}{s-1}\right)
330	 =\gamma_ER_f+P_f'(1)=B_f+\frac32R_f.               \tag{26}
331	\]
332	This proves that the definitions of \(R_f\) and \(B_f\) have the
333	specified values without any unspecified remainder in a Laurent
334	expansion.
335	
336	At \(s=-1/2\), every local factor of \(H_f\) is strictly positive:
337	\[
338	M_p(-1/2)
339	 =(1-p^{-1})\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)>0. \tag{27}
340	\]
341	The nonnegativity and strict positivity needed here are exactly (5).
342	The series of absolute deviations of these factors from \(1\)
343	converges by (11)--(12) with \(\sigma=-1/2\). A convergent product
344	of positive factors with summable absolute deviations has positive
345	limit: after finitely many factors, \(|M_p(-1/2)-1|\le1/2\), and
346	then \(|\log M_p(-1/2)|\le2|M_p(-1/2)-1|\).
347	Consequently \(H_f(-1/2)>0\). Combining this with (23) proves
348	\[
349	K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)>0.                \tag{28}
350	\]
351	For clarity, the explicit Euler product in this constant is
352	\[
353	K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)
354	 \prod_p\left\{
355	 (1-2/p^2)(1-1/p)
356	 \bigl[a_p+(b_p-a_p)\sqrt p+(c_p-b_p)p\bigr]
357	 \right\}.                                       \tag{29}
358	\]
359	The factors inside braces are kept grouped at each prime; their
360	absolute convergence is precisely the convergence just proved for
361	\(H_f(-1/2)\). The pole of \(\zeta(2s+2)\) contributes a factor
362	\(1/2\) to its residue. Equations (23)--(24) therefore also give
363	\[
364	\operatorname*{Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
365	 =\frac12\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)=-\frac3{16}K_f.       \tag{30}
366	\]
367	The only possible poles in the stated region are \(1\) and \(-1/2\).
368	Both are genuine: the local factors of \(P_f(1)\) are positive with
369	summable absolute deviations, and (28) makes (30) nonzero.
370	
371	It remains to identify the common density coefficient. Substitution
372	of (4) into \(L_p(1)\) gives the exact identity
373	\[
374	\begin{aligned}
375	L_p(1)
376	 &=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}{p}+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}\\
377	 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}
378	       +\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}\\
379	 &=(1-p^{-2})^2
380	 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right].
381	                                                               \tag{31}
382	\end{aligned}
383	\]
384	Let
385	\[
386	T_p=\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}.
387	\]
388	Since \(p^2-1\ge3p^2/4\), (1) bounds the term for each prime by
389	\[
390	0\le T_p\le\frac{16C_0}{9}(p^{-4}+p^{-3}).          \tag{32}
391	\]
392	The sum over the infinitely many primes \(p>N\) is therefore bounded
393	explicitly by
394	\[
395	\sum_{p>N}T_p
396	 \le\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right). \tag{33}
397	\]
398	This proves absolute convergence of the product of \(1+T_p\).
399	The product of \((1-p^{-2})^2\) is absolutely convergent as well,
400	since the absolute deviation of its factor from \(1\) is
401	\(2p^{-2}-p^{-4}\le2p^{-2}\), with prime tail at most \(2/N\).
402	Multiplying (31) over the primes and using the Euler product for
403	\(\zeta(2)\) proves
404	\[
405	R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p
406	 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right]. \tag{34}
407	\]
408	
409	Finally, the Chinese remainder theorem gives
410	\(\rho(mn)=\rho(m)\rho(n)\) for \((m,n)=1\): the bijection between
411	residues modulo \(mn\) and pairs of residues modulo \(m,n\) restricts
412	to a bijection between the respective polynomial roots. Put
413	\[
414	v(r)=
415	\begin{cases}
416	\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(r)\rho(r)}r
417	             \prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2},
418	 &\text{if no prime cube divides }r,\\
419	0,&\text{otherwise}.
420	\end{cases}
421	\]
422	This is a nonnegative multiplicative function with \(v(1)=1\).
423	Its first two prime-power values are
424	\[
425	v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
426	v(p^2)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2}.          \tag{35}
427	\]
428	For \(e\ge3\), its value \(v(p^e)\) is zero.
429	For the primes at most \(N\), the finite product of
430	\(1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p\) expands into a finite nonnegative sum over
431	the \(3^{\pi(N)}\) integers obtained by choosing each such prime's
432	exponent from \(\{0,1,2\}\). These sets increase to all integers
433	with no prime-cube divisor. By (32) and (2), their sums are bounded
434	by
435	\[
436	\prod_p(1+T_p)\le
437	 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac13+\frac12\right)\right)
438	 =\exp(40C_0/27).                                  \tag{36}
439	\]
440	Monotone convergence thus proves absolute convergence and the
441	Euler-product identity
442	\[
443	\sum_{r\ge1}v(r)=\prod_p(1+T_p).
444	\]
445	Explicitly, the omitted sum over the infinitely many integers having
446	a prime divisor greater than \(N\) is at most
447	\[
448	\exp(40C_0/27)
449	 \left[
450	 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}
451	                \left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right)\right)-1
452	 \right].                                         \tag{37}
453	\]
454	Indeed the omitted sum is exactly
455	\[
456	\left(\prod_{p\le N}(1+T_p)\right)
457	\left(\prod_{p>N}(1+T_p)-1\right),
458	\]
459	so (3), (33), and (36) give (37).
460	The definition of \(\lambda(r)\) in the statement satisfies
461	\(\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=\zeta(2)^{-2}v(r)\). Equations (34)--(35)
462	therefore give the required identity
463	\[
464	R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
465	\]
466	All the Euler products specifying \(R_f\) or \(K_f\) have had their
467	absolute convergence established above.
468	
469	No external literature or numerical checks were used in this proof.
470
