Put \(A_d=[t^d]f(t)\ne0\), and fix
\[
C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|,1\}.
\]
For every prime \(p\nmid A_d\), reduction modulo \(p\) is a nonzero
polynomial of degree \(d\), so the factor theorem gives at most \(d\)
roots. If \(p\mid A_d\), the bound
\(\rho(p)\le p\le |A_d|\) applies. Each residue class modulo \(p\) has
exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\). Consequently,
\[
0\le\rho(p)\le\min\{C_0,p\},\qquad
0\le\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)\le C_0p.                 \tag{1}
\]
These bounds require no assumption on the content, discriminant, or
factorization of \(f\).

We will use the following explicit summation estimate. If \(u>1\) and
\(N\ge1\) is an integer, comparison with an integral gives
\[
\sum_{p>N}p^{-u}\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-u}
\le\int_N^\infty t^{-u}\,dt
=\frac{N^{1-u}}{u-1}.                              \tag{2}
\]
Both sums in (2) have infinitely many possible indices. A bound
\(k p^{-u}\) for each prime therefore has total at most
\(kN^{1-u}/(u-1)\) after summing over \(p>N\). In particular, the sum over
all primes is at most \(k/(u-1)\).
If local factors are \(1+e_p(s)\), the estimate
\[
\left|\prod_{p>N}(1+e_p(s))-1\right|
\le \exp\!\left(\sum_{p>N}|e_p(s)|\right)-1          \tag{3}
\]
follows first for finite products by expansion and then for their limits.
Thus all the prime-sum tail estimates below also give explicit product
tail estimates. Uniform summability of \(|e_p|\) on compact sets gives
local uniform convergence to a holomorphic function, since the finite
products are holomorphic.

For brevity put \(q_p=1-2/p^2\), and introduce the three coefficients
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_p&=q_pa_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
\beta_p&=q_p(b_p-a_p)=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}
                              -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
\delta_p&=q_p(c_p-b_p)=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
\]
By (1),
\[
\begin{gathered}
0<q_p\le\alpha_p\le1,\qquad
0\le\beta_p\le C_0p^{-3},\qquad
0\le\delta_p\le p^{-2},\\
|\alpha_p-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3},\qquad
\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}.                 \tag{5}
\end{gathered}
\]
In particular, \(b_p-a_p\ge0\) and \(c_p-b_p\ge0\).

The local factor \(w_p(h)\) in \(W_f(h)\) is, according as
\(v_p(h)=0,1\) or at least \(2\),
\[
w_p(h)=\alpha_p,\quad
\alpha_p+\beta_p,\quad
\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p,
\]
respectively. Alternatively, the elementary bound
\(0\le\rho(p^j)\le p^j\), including \(j=0\), gives directly
\[
1-\frac2{p^2}\le w_p(h)\le1-\frac1{p^2},\qquad
|w_p(h)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}.                          \tag{6}
\]
The prime tail of the last bound is at most \(2/N\) by (2), uniformly
in \(h\). Every factor is at least \(1/2\). For \(1/2\le t\le1\),
\(-\log t\le2(1-t)\); hence
\[
\sum_p|\log w_p(h)|\le4\sum_pp^{-2}\le4.
\]
It follows that the product defining \(W_f(h)\) is absolutely convergent
and \(0<W_f(h)\le1\). For \(s=\sigma+it\) with \(\sigma>1\), this gives
\[
\sum_{h\ge1}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_{h\ge1}h^{-\sigma}<\infty.
\]
More explicitly, the sum of the errors over the infinitely many indices
\(h>N\) is bounded by
\[
\sum_{h>N}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|
\le\sum_{h>N}h^{-\sigma}
\le\frac{N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                  \tag{7}
\]
This proves the asserted absolute convergence of \(D_f\).

Write
\[
L_p(s)=q_pB_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s}.
\]
On the closed half-plane \(\Re s\ge\sigma\), (5) gives the bound for
each individual prime
\[
|L_p(s)-1|
\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}.       \tag{8}
\]
If \(\sigma>-1/2\), all four exponents exceed \(1\). Summing (8) over
the infinitely many primes \(p>N\), using (2) separately for its four
terms, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{p>N}|L_p(s)-1|\le E_P(N;\sigma)
={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
 +\frac{N^{-1-2\sigma}}{1+2\sigma}.                 \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
Every power of \(N\) on the right has negative exponent. Equations
(3) and (9) prove absolute and locally uniform convergence of \(P_f\)
on \(\Re s>-1/2\). They also prove its holomorphy there.

The local factor in \(H_f\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_p(s)&=(1-p^{-2s-2})L_p(s)\\
 &=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}
 +(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2})p^{-2s}
 -\beta_pp^{-2}p^{-3s}-\delta_pp^{-2}p^{-4s}.         \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient where cancellation is needed is exactly
\[
\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}
 =-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}
                         -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6},
\]
so its absolute value is at most
\(C_0p^{-3}+2p^{-4}+C_0p^{-5}\). Thus, for \(\Re s\ge\sigma\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|M_p(s)-1|\le{}&2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}
 +C_0p^{-3-2\sigma}+2p^{-4-2\sigma}\\
 &+C_0p^{-5-2\sigma}+C_0p^{-5-3\sigma}
 +p^{-4-4\sigma}.                                  \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(\sigma>-3/4\), the eight exponents on the right are, respectively,
\[
2,\ 3,\ 3+\sigma,\ 3+2\sigma,\ 4+2\sigma,
\ 5+2\sigma,\ 5+3\sigma,\ 4+4\sigma,
\]
and each is greater than \(1\). The sum over the infinitely many primes
\(p>N\), before summation bounded prime by prime by (11), is after
summation bounded by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{p>N}|M_p(s)-1|\le E_H(N;\sigma)
={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-2\sigma}}{2+2\sigma}\\
 &+\frac{2N^{-3-2\sigma}}{3+2\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-2\sigma}}{4+2\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-3\sigma}}{4+3\sigma}
 +\frac{N^{-3-4\sigma}}{3+4\sigma}.                 \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]
All denominators in (12) are positive, and all powers of \(N\) have
negative exponents in this range. Equations (3) and (12) prove absolute
and locally uniform convergence, and holomorphy, of \(H_f\) on
\(\Re s>-3/4\). For every real \(t\), the bound
\(|M_p(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(|M_p(\sigma+it)-1|)\) also proves
\[
|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le \exp(E_H(1;\sigma)).             \tag{13}
\]
Thus one may take \(C(f,\sigma)=\exp(E_H(1;\sigma))\), with every
term in its exponent specified in (12).

We next identify the Dirichlet series. The positive number
\[
A=\prod_p\alpha_p
\]
exists by (5), or by (6) with \(h=1\). Define
\(u(h)=W_f(h)/A\). Only the primes dividing \(h\) change a factor of
this quotient, so \(u\) is multiplicative and
\[
u(1)=1,\qquad u(p)=\frac{b_p}{a_p},\qquad
u(p^e)=\frac{c_p}{a_p}\quad(e\ge2).
\]
In particular \(0<u(h)\le A^{-1}\). For \(\Re s>1\), its local series is
\[
\sum_{e\ge0}u(p^e)p^{-es}
 =1+\frac{b_p}{a_p}p^{-s}
       +\frac{c_p}{a_p}\frac{p^{-2s}}{1-p^{-s}}
 =\frac{B_p(s)}{a_p(1-p^{-s})}.                    \tag{14}
\]
To justify multiplication of these series, first include only primes
\(p\le N\). Their finite product expands into the sum over integers
whose prime factors are all at most \(N\). Every omitted integer is
greater than \(N\). The omitted sum has infinitely many possible
indices, each term has modulus at most \(A^{-1}h^{-\sigma}\), and its
total modulus is at most
\[
\frac{A^{-1}N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                \tag{15}
\]
This tends to zero. Multiplying (14) over all primes therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_f(s)
 &=\lim_{N\to\infty}
 \left(\prod_{p\le N}\frac{L_p(s)}{1-p^{-s}}\right)
 \left(\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p\right)\\
 &=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad \Re s>1.                 \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the Euler product for \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\) follows
by unique prime factorization: its finite-prime expansion omits only
integers \(n>N\), whose total absolute contribution is at most
\(N^{1-\sigma}/(\sigma-1)\). The extra tail product in (16) tends to
\(1\), with explicit bound
\[
\left|\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p-1\right|
 \le \exp\!\left(\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}\right)-1. \tag{17}
\]

For \(\Re s>-1/2\), the Euler product for \(\zeta(2s+2)\) is
absolutely convergent. Its reciprocal product is nonzero, since
\(|p^{-2s-2}|<1\) and
\(\sum_p|p^{-2s-2}|<\infty\). Multiplying the absolutely convergent
products defining \(P_f\) and \(H_f\) gives
\[
P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\quad(\Re s>-1/2).          \tag{18}
\]
In particular, (16) proves both required identities on \(\Re s>1\).

For completeness, the zeta-function facts needed for continuation and
signs can all be derived directly. For \(\Re w>1\), integrating the
counting function of the positive integers gives
\[
\zeta(w)=w\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-w-1}\,dx
 =\frac1{w-1}+\frac12
       -w\int_1^\infty(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx.     \tag{19}
\]
Let
\(\mathcal B_2(x)=\{x\}^2-\{x\}+1/6\).
This function is continuous at integers, is bounded in absolute value
by \(1/6\), and has derivative \(2(\{x\}-1/2)\) between consecutive
integers. More explicitly, for an integer \(T\ge2\), integration by
parts over the \(T-1\) intervals between \(1\) and \(T\) gives the
exact identity
\[
\int_1^T(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx
 =\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}
  +\frac{w+1}{2}\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.
\]
The internal endpoint terms cancel exactly. The upper endpoint
term, after multiplication by \(-w\), has modulus
\(|w|T^{-\Re w-1}/12\), which tends to zero for \(\Re w>1\).
Substitution in (19) therefore yields
\[
\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}
 -\frac{w(w+1)}2
       \int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.    \tag{20}
\]
The integral is holomorphic for \(\Re w>-1\). Explicitly, its tail
past \(T\ge1\), including the coefficient in (20), has absolute value
at most
\[
\frac{|w(w+1)|}{12(\Re w+1)}T^{-\Re w-1}.           \tag{21}
\]
For each nonnegative integer \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the
integrand with respect to \(w\) is dominated on \(\Re w\ge\eta>-1\)
by \((\log x)^m x^{-\eta-2}/6\), whose integral is
\(m!/[6(\eta+1)^{m+1}]\). These bounds justify holomorphy and the
continuation in (20), with its sole pole at \(w=1\) and residue \(1\).

We also record the constant term at that pole. For an integer \(N\ge1\),
the same counting-function integration gives, initially for
\(\Re w>1\) and then by continuation for \(\Re w>0\),
\[
\zeta(w)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}
       -w\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-w-1}\,dx.           \tag{22}
\]
The finite sum has exactly \(N\) terms. The final integral, including
its coefficient, is bounded by
\(|w|N^{-\Re w}/\Re w\). Subtracting \(1/(w-1)\) and taking
\(w\to1\) gives
\[
\lim_{w\to1}\left(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\right)
 =\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n-\log N
       -\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-2}\,dx.
\]
The integral is between \(0\) and \(1/N\). Taking \(N\to\infty\),
the right side is Euler's constant \(\gamma_E\), by its defining
harmonic-sum limit.

Equation (20) gives \(\zeta(0)=-1/2\). At \(w=-1/2\) it gives
\[
\zeta(-1/2)=-\frac5{24}
       +\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-3/2}\,dx.
\]
The integral has absolute value at most
\((1/6)\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx=1/3\). Hence
\[
-\frac14\le\zeta(-1/2)\le-\frac16<0.              \tag{23}
\]

For \(\Re s>-3/4\), the two arguments \(s\) and \(2s+2\) in
\[
\widetilde D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)         \tag{24}
\]
satisfy \(\Re s>-1\) and \(\Re(2s+2)>1/2>-1\).
Thus (20) and the holomorphy of \(H_f\) prove that (24) is
meromorphic throughout this region. It agrees with \(D_f\) on
\(\Re s>1\) by (16) and (18), so it is the claimed continuation.
We henceforth use the notation \(D_f\) for this continuation.

At \(s=0\),
\[
L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2},\qquad
P_f(0)=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})=\frac1{\zeta(2)}.
\]
The equality \(D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)\) extends meromorphically to
\(\Re s>-1/2\) by (18) and (24). Both factors are regular at zero,
so
\[
D_f(0)=\zeta(0)P_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}.          \tag{25}
\]

At \(s=1\), \(P_f\) is holomorphic. With \(R_f=P_f(1)\), equations
(16) and (22) show
\[
\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}D_f(s)=R_f,\qquad
\lim_{s\to1}\left(D_f(s)-\frac{R_f}{s-1}\right)
 =\gamma_ER_f+P_f'(1)=B_f+\frac32R_f.               \tag{26}
\]
This proves that the definitions of \(R_f\) and \(B_f\) have the
specified values without any unspecified remainder in a Laurent
expansion.

At \(s=-1/2\), every local factor of \(H_f\) is strictly positive:
\[
M_p(-1/2)
 =(1-p^{-1})\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)>0. \tag{27}
\]
The nonnegativity and strict positivity needed here are exactly (5).
The series of absolute deviations of these factors from \(1\)
converges by (11)--(12) with \(\sigma=-1/2\). A convergent product
of positive factors with summable absolute deviations has positive
limit: after finitely many factors, \(|M_p(-1/2)-1|\le1/2\), and
then \(|\log M_p(-1/2)|\le2|M_p(-1/2)-1|\).
Consequently \(H_f(-1/2)>0\). Combining this with (23) proves
\[
K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)>0.                \tag{28}
\]
For clarity, the explicit Euler product in this constant is
\[
K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)
 \prod_p\left\{
 (1-2/p^2)(1-1/p)
 \bigl[a_p+(b_p-a_p)\sqrt p+(c_p-b_p)p\bigr]
 \right\}.                                       \tag{29}
\]
The factors inside braces are kept grouped at each prime; their
absolute convergence is precisely the convergence just proved for
\(H_f(-1/2)\). The pole of \(\zeta(2s+2)\) contributes a factor
\(1/2\) to its residue. Equations (23)--(24) therefore also give
\[
\operatorname*{Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
 =\frac12\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)=-\frac3{16}K_f.       \tag{30}
\]
The only possible poles in the stated region are \(1\) and \(-1/2\).
Both are genuine: the local factors of \(P_f(1)\) are positive with
summable absolute deviations, and (28) makes (30) nonzero.

It remains to identify the common density coefficient. Substitution
of (4) into \(L_p(1)\) gives the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_p(1)
 &=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}{p}+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}\\
 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}
       +\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}\\
 &=(1-p^{-2})^2
 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right].
                                                               \tag{31}
\end{aligned}
\]
Let
\[
T_p=\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}.
\]
Since \(p^2-1\ge3p^2/4\), (1) bounds the term for each prime by
\[
0\le T_p\le\frac{16C_0}{9}(p^{-4}+p^{-3}).          \tag{32}
\]
The sum over the infinitely many primes \(p>N\) is therefore bounded
explicitly by
\[
\sum_{p>N}T_p
 \le\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right). \tag{33}
\]
This proves absolute convergence of the product of \(1+T_p\).
The product of \((1-p^{-2})^2\) is absolutely convergent as well,
since the absolute deviation of its factor from \(1\) is
\(2p^{-2}-p^{-4}\le2p^{-2}\), with prime tail at most \(2/N\).
Multiplying (31) over the primes and using the Euler product for
\(\zeta(2)\) proves
\[
R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p
 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right]. \tag{34}
\]

Finally, the Chinese remainder theorem gives
\(\rho(mn)=\rho(m)\rho(n)\) for \((m,n)=1\): the bijection between
residues modulo \(mn\) and pairs of residues modulo \(m,n\) restricts
to a bijection between the respective polynomial roots. Put
\[
v(r)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(r)\rho(r)}r
             \prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2},
 &\text{if no prime cube divides }r,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is a nonnegative multiplicative function with \(v(1)=1\).
Its first two prime-power values are
\[
v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
v(p^2)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2}.          \tag{35}
\]
For \(e\ge3\), its value \(v(p^e)\) is zero.
For the primes at most \(N\), the finite product of
\(1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p\) expands into a finite nonnegative sum over
the \(3^{\pi(N)}\) integers obtained by choosing each such prime's
exponent from \(\{0,1,2\}\). These sets increase to all integers
with no prime-cube divisor. By (32) and (2), their sums are bounded
by
\[
\prod_p(1+T_p)\le
 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac13+\frac12\right)\right)
 =\exp(40C_0/27).                                  \tag{36}
\]
Monotone convergence thus proves absolute convergence and the
Euler-product identity
\[
\sum_{r\ge1}v(r)=\prod_p(1+T_p).
\]
Explicitly, the omitted sum over the infinitely many integers having
a prime divisor greater than \(N\) is at most
\[
\exp(40C_0/27)
 \left[
 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}
                \left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right)\right)-1
 \right].                                         \tag{37}
\]
Indeed the omitted sum is exactly
\[
\left(\prod_{p\le N}(1+T_p)\right)
\left(\prod_{p>N}(1+T_p)-1\right),
\]
so (3), (33), and (36) give (37).
The definition of \(\lambda(r)\) in the statement satisfies
\(\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=\zeta(2)^{-2}v(r)\). Equations (34)--(35)
therefore give the required identity
\[
R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
\]
All the Euler products specifying \(R_f\) or \(K_f\) have had their
absolute convergence established above.

No external literature or numerical checks were used in this proof.

1	# Proof of P1
2	
3	Write \(e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)\), and take logarithms to base \(e\). All sums over integers below are over positive integers unless another range is specified. We prove the assertions directly; no external literature or dependency proposition is used.
4	
5	## Existence and evaluation of the density
6	
7	For every positive integer \(n\), prime factorization gives
8	\[
9	\sum_{m^2\mid n}\mu(m)
10	=\prod_{p^2\mid n}(1-1)=\mu^2(n),
11	\tag{1}
12	\]
13	where an empty product equals one. Fix \(q\geq1\) and \(l\in\mathbb Z\). For \(x\geq1\), put \(M=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) and \(d_m=(m^2,q)\). The simultaneous congruences
14	\[
15	n\equiv l\pmod q,\qquad n\equiv0\pmod{m^2}
16	\]
17	are soluble precisely when \(d_m\mid l\). Indeed, writing \(n=m^2k\) reduces them to a linear congruence in \(k\); division by \(d_m\) leaves a coefficient coprime to \(q/d_m\). When soluble, the solutions form one residue class modulo \(qm^2/d_m\). The number of its members in \([1,x]\) differs from \(xd_m/(qm^2)\) by at most one. Consequently (1) gives
18	\[
19	Q(x;q,l)=\frac{x}{q}
20	\sum_{\substack{m\leq M\\d_m\mid l}}
21	\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}+E_1,
22	\qquad |E_1|\leq M.
23	\tag{2}
24	\]
25	Here each counting error has absolute value at most one, and there are at most \(M\) terms, so their sum has absolute value at most \(M\).
26	
27	The series
28	\[
29	D(q,l)=\frac1q\sum_{\substack{m\geq1\\d_m\mid l}}
30	\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}
31	\tag{3}
32	\]
33	converges absolutely: each summand has absolute value at most \(m^{-2}\), since \(d_m\leq q\). The infinite omitted tail in (2), after multiplication by \(x\), has absolute value at most
34	\[
35	x\sum_{m>M}\frac1{m^2}
36	\leq x\int_M^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=\frac{x}{M}.
37	\tag{4}
38	\]
39	Since \(\sqrt{x}/2\leq M\leq\sqrt{x}\), equations (2)--(4) prove the explicit estimate
40	\[
41	|Q(x;q,l)-xD(q,l)|
42	\leq M+\frac{x}{M}\leq3\sqrt{x},
43	\qquad x\geq1.
44	\tag{5}
45	\]
46	Dividing by \(x\) and letting \(x\) tend to infinity proves that the density from `problem.md` exists and equals (3).
47	
48	We will use the elementary Euler identity
49	\[
50	c=\zeta(2)^{-1}=\prod_p(1-p^{-2}).
51	\tag{6}
52	\]
53	To justify it here, expanding \(\prod_{p\leq z}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\) gives the sum of \(m^{-2}\) over integers all of whose prime factors are at most \(z\). These sums increase to \(\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\zeta(2)\), because every integer has finitely many prime factors. Taking reciprocals gives (6).
54	
55	For a prime \(p\), let \(t=v_p(q)\). The summand in (3) vanishes unless \(m\) is squarefree. The choice to include \(p\) in such an \(m\) contributes
56	\(-p^{\min(2,t)-2}\), and is allowed precisely when
57	\(p^{\min(2,t)}\mid l\). Thus the local factor in \(qg(q,l)\) is
58	\[
59	\begin{cases}
60	1-p^{-2},&t=0,\\
61	1,&t=1,\ p\nmid l,\\
62	1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
63	1,&t\geq2,\ p^2\nmid l,\\
64	0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l.
65	\end{cases}
66	\tag{7}
67	\]
68	This Euler expansion is justified by the absolute convergence of (3); equivalently, expand over finitely many primes and pass to the absolutely convergent series. The divisibility conditions in (7) also apply to \(l=0\).
69	
70	If some \(p^2\) divides both \(q\) and \(l\), (7) gives \(g(q,l)=0\). In every other case, combining (6) and (7) gives exactly
71	\[
72	g(q,l)=\frac cq
73	\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}
74	\prod_{\substack{p\parallel q\\p\mid l}}(1-p^{-1}).
75	\tag{8}
76	\]
77	Every local factor in (7) lies in \([0,1]\). Their product therefore lies in \([0,1]\), proving
78	\[
79	0\leq g(q,l)\leq\frac1q.
80	\tag{9}
81	\]
82	
83	## The finite second-moment identity
84	
85	Let
86	\[
87	L(r)=\varphi(r)G(r)^2,
88	\qquad \lambda(r)=c^2L(r).
89	\]
90	The function \(L\) is multiplicative. Its prime-power values are
91	\[
92	L(p)=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
93	L(p^2)=\frac{p(p-1)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
94	L(p^j)=0\quad(j\geq3).
95	\tag{10}
96	\]
97	These formulas follow from counting the \(p^j-p^{j-1}\) residues coprime to \(p^j\); multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) follows from the Chinese remainder theorem.
98	
99	For \(t\geq1\), define a function on residues modulo \(p^t\) by
100	\[
101	b_{p,t}(l)=
102	\begin{cases}
103	1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
104	0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l,\\
105	1,&\text{otherwise}.
106	\end{cases}
107	\]
108	Equations (7)--(8), including their zero cases, give
109	\[
110	qg(q,l)=c\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
111	(1-p^{-2})^{-1}b_{p,t}(l).
112	\tag{11}
113	\]
114	For \(t=1\), there are \(p-1\) residues with \(b_{p,1}=1\) and one with \(b_{p,1}=1-p^{-1}\). Hence
115	\[
116	\begin{aligned}
117	(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1p\sum_{l\bmod p}b_{p,1}(l)^2
118	&=(1-p^{-2})^{-2}
119	\left(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^3}\right)\\
120	&=\frac{p^4-2p^2+p}{(p^2-1)^2}\\
121	&=1+\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2}=1+L(p).
122	\end{aligned}
123	\tag{12}
124	\]
125	For \(t\geq2\), precisely \(p^{t-2}\) of the \(p^t\) residues have \(b_{p,t}=0\), and the other \(p^t-p^{t-2}\) have value one. Therefore
126	\[
127	\begin{aligned}
128	(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1{p^t}
129	\sum_{l\bmod p^t}b_{p,t}(l)^2
130	&=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\\
131	&=1+\frac1{p^2-1}\\
132	&=1+L(p)+L(p^2).
133	\end{aligned}
134	\tag{13}
135	\]
136	The last equality uses
137	\((p-1)+p(p-1)=p^2-1\).
138	
139	The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the \(q\) residues modulo \(q\) with the Cartesian product of the residue sets modulo its prime-power factors. Averaging the square of (11) consequently factors into the local averages (12)--(13). With empty products understood when \(q=1\), this yields
140	\[
141	\begin{aligned}
142	q\sum_{l=1}^qg(q,l)^2
143	&=\frac1q\sum_{l=1}^q(qg(q,l))^2\\
144	&=c^2\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
145	\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^tL(p^j)\right)\\
146	&=c^2\sum_{r\mid q}L(r)
147	=\sum_{r\mid q}\lambda(r).
148	\end{aligned}
149	\tag{14}
150	\]
151	
152	## Absolute summability and explicit tail estimates
153	
154	The support of \(L\) consists of integers with no prime exponent exceeding two. Every such integer has a unique representation
155	\[
156	r=ab^2,
157	\qquad a,b\text{ squarefree},\quad(a,b)=1.
158	\tag{15}
159	\]
160	For every prime \(p\geq2\), set
161	\[
162	A_p=\frac{p^3}{(p-1)(p+1)^2}.
163	\]
164	The denominator minus the numerator equals \(p^2-p-1\), which is at least one for \(p\geq2\). Thus \(0<A_p\leq1\), and (10) becomes
165	\[
166	L(p)=\frac{A_p}{p^3},\qquad
167	L(p^2)=\frac{A_p}{p^2}.
168	\]
169	Multiplying these inequalities over the prime factors in (15) proves
170	\[
171	0\leq\lambda(ab^2)\leq\frac{c^2}{a^3b^2}.
172	\tag{16}
173	\]
174	Dropping the restrictions on \(a,b\) only increases these nonnegative sums. In particular
175	\[
176	\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
177	\leq c^2\left(\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-3}\right)
178	\left(\sum_{b\geq1}b^{-2}\right)
179	\leq3c^2<\infty,
180	\tag{17}
181	\]
182	where the two series are bounded by
183	\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}dt=3/2\) and
184	\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt=2\), respectively.
185	
186	We can now evaluate the sum by its absolutely convergent Euler product. Equation (10) gives
187	\[
188	1+L(p)+L(p^2)
189	=1+\frac1{p^2-1}=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}.
190	\]
191	Consequently (6) implies
192	\[
193	\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
194	=c^2\prod_p(1+L(p)+L(p^2))
195	=c^2\zeta(2)=c.
196	\tag{18}
197	\]
198	
199	For every real \(T>0\), we have the explicit bound
200	\[
201	\sum_{b>T}\frac1{b^2}\leq\frac2T.
202	\tag{19}
203	\]
204	For \(T\geq1\), putting \(N=\lfloor T\rfloor\geq T/2\) bounds this infinite tail by
205	\(\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N\leq2/T\).
206	For \(0<T<1\), the sum is at most \(2\), which is at most \(2/T\).
207	For any \(R>0\), (16) and then (19), with \(T=\sqrt{R/a}\), give
208	\[
209	\begin{aligned}
210	\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)
211	&\leq c^2\sum_{a\geq1}\frac1{a^3}
212	\sum_{b>\sqrt{R/a}}\frac1{b^2}\\
213	&\leq2c^2R^{-1/2}\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}\\
214	&\leq\frac{10}{3}R^{-1/2}.
215	\end{aligned}
216	\tag{20}
217	\]
218	For each \(a\), the inner infinite sum before summation over \(a\) is at most \(2\sqrt{a/R}\). Its contribution after multiplication by \(c^2a^{-3}\) is at most \(2c^2R^{-1/2}a^{-5/2}\). The final bound uses \(c\leq1\) and
219	\[
220	\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}
221	\leq1+\int_1^\infty t^{-5/2}dt=\frac53.
222	\tag{21}
223	\]
224	
225	Multiplication of (16) by \(ab^2\) gives
226	\(ab^2\lambda(ab^2)\leq c^2a^{-2}\). Thus
227	\[
228	\begin{aligned}
229	\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r)
230	&\leq c^2\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}\frac1{a^2}
231	\sum_{1\leq b\leq\sqrt{R/a}}1\\
232	&\leq c^2R^{1/2}\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}a^{-5/2}
233	\leq\frac53R^{1/2}.
234	\end{aligned}
235	\tag{22}
236	\]
237	For each \(a\leq R\), the inner sum has
238	\(\lfloor\sqrt{R/a}\rfloor\leq\sqrt{R/a}\) terms, each contributing at most \(c^2a^{-2}\). Its total is at most \(c^2R^{1/2}a^{-5/2}\). Summing over the \(\lfloor R\rfloor\) possible values of \(a\), and applying (21), gives the last inequality in (22).
239	
240	For \(R\geq2\), \(\log(2R)\geq\log4>1\). Therefore (20) and (22) imply both bounds requested in the statement, with the same absolute constant \(C=10/3\). They also prove the stronger versions without logarithmic factors.
241	
242	## The Ramanujan series
243	
244	There are \(\varphi(r)\) terms in the defining sum for \(c_r(n)\), each of absolute value one. Hence, for every integer \(n\),
245	\[
246	|c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
247	\sum_{r\geq1}|\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)|
248	\leq\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)=c.
249	\tag{23}
250	\]
251	This proves absolute convergence, with a bound uniform in \(n\).
252	
253	For completeness, the multiplicativity needed to evaluate the series follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem. If \((s,t)=1\), choose integers \(u,v\) with \(tu\equiv1\pmod s\) and \(sv\equiv1\pmod t\). A unit residue \(a\pmod{st}\) corresponding to unit residues \(b\pmod s\), \(d\pmod t\) satisfies
254	\[
255	\frac{a}{st}\equiv\frac{bu}{s}+\frac{dv}{t}\pmod1.
256	\]
257	Summing the resulting exponential identity over \(b,d\), and using the permutations of unit residues induced by multiplication by \(u,v\), gives
258	\[
259	c_{st}(n)=c_s(n)c_t(n).
260	\tag{24}
261	\]
262	
263	The finite geometric sum satisfies
264	\[
265	\sum_{a=1}^k e(an/k)=k\,\boldsymbol1_{k\mid n}.
266	\]
267	Subtracting the term for the zero residue modulo \(p\) gives
268	\(c_p(n)=p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}-1\).
269	Subtracting the sum over residues divisible by \(p\) from the full sum modulo \(p^2\) gives
270	\[
271	c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}
272	-p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}.
273	\]
274	Adding these two exact identities yields
275	\[
276	c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
277	\tag{25}
278	\]
279	By (23)--(24), the absolutely convergent series has the Euler expansion
280	\[
281	\sum_{r\geq1}\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)
282	=c^2\prod_p
283	\left(1+\frac{c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)}{(p^2-1)^2}\right).
284	\tag{26}
285	\]
286	Using (6), absorb the factor \((1-p^{-2})^2\) of \(c^2\) into each local factor. If \(p^2\nmid n\), (25) gives
287	\[
288	(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1-\frac1{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
289	=\frac{(p^2-1)^2-1}{p^4}
290	=1-\frac2{p^2}.
291	\tag{27}
292	\]
293	If \(p^2\mid n\), it gives
294	\[
295	(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1+\frac{p^2-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
296	=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2}
297	=1-\frac1{p^2}.
298	\tag{28}
299	\]
300	All these product operations are legitimate: (26) is justified by absolute convergence, and (6) converges. The product \(\prod_p(1-2/p^2)\) converges to a positive number as well. Indeed, for \(0\leq u\leq1/2\),
301	\(-\log(1-u)=\int_0^u(1-t)^{-1}dt\leq2u\), so
302	\(\sum_p|\log(1-2/p^2)|\leq4\sum_p p^{-2}<\infty\).
303	
304	Finally, when \(n\geq1\), only finitely many primes satisfy \(p^2\mid n\). Replacing the factors (27) by (28) for those primes multiplies the baseline product by
305	\[
306	\frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.
307	\]
308	Thus (26) equals precisely
309	\[
310	\boxed{\displaystyle
311	\mathfrak S(n)=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
312	\prod_{p^2\mid n}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.}
313	\]
314	This proves every assertion of P1.
315	
316	No numerical checks or external sources were used.
317

# Proof of P1

Write \(e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)\), and take logarithms to base \(e\). All sums over integers below are over positive integers unless another range is specified. We prove the assertions directly; no external literature or dependency proposition is used.

## Existence and evaluation of the density

For every positive integer \(n\), prime factorization gives
\[
\sum_{m^2\mid n}\mu(m)
=\prod_{p^2\mid n}(1-1)=\mu^2(n),
\tag{1}
\]
where an empty product equals one. Fix \(q\geq1\) and \(l\in\mathbb Z\). For \(x\geq1\), put \(M=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) and \(d_m=(m^2,q)\). The simultaneous congruences
\[
n\equiv l\pmod q,\qquad n\equiv0\pmod{m^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(d_m\mid l\). Indeed, writing \(n=m^2k\) reduces them to a linear congruence in \(k\); division by \(d_m\) leaves a coefficient coprime to \(q/d_m\). When soluble, the solutions form one residue class modulo \(qm^2/d_m\). The number of its members in \([1,x]\) differs from \(xd_m/(qm^2)\) by at most one. Consequently (1) gives
\[
Q(x;q,l)=\frac{x}{q}
\sum_{\substack{m\leq M\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}+E_1,
\qquad |E_1|\leq M.
\tag{2}
\]
Here each counting error has absolute value at most one, and there are at most \(M\) terms, so their sum has absolute value at most \(M\).

The series
\[
D(q,l)=\frac1q\sum_{\substack{m\geq1\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}
\tag{3}
\]
converges absolutely: each summand has absolute value at most \(m^{-2}\), since \(d_m\leq q\). The infinite omitted tail in (2), after multiplication by \(x\), has absolute value at most
\[
x\sum_{m>M}\frac1{m^2}
\leq x\int_M^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=\frac{x}{M}.
\tag{4}
\]
Since \(\sqrt{x}/2\leq M\leq\sqrt{x}\), equations (2)--(4) prove the explicit estimate
\[
|Q(x;q,l)-xD(q,l)|
\leq M+\frac{x}{M}\leq3\sqrt{x},
\qquad x\geq1.
\tag{5}
\]
Dividing by \(x\) and letting \(x\) tend to infinity proves that the density from `problem.md` exists and equals (3).

We will use the elementary Euler identity
\[
c=\zeta(2)^{-1}=\prod_p(1-p^{-2}).
\tag{6}
\]
To justify it here, expanding \(\prod_{p\leq z}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\) gives the sum of \(m^{-2}\) over integers all of whose prime factors are at most \(z\). These sums increase to \(\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\zeta(2)\), because every integer has finitely many prime factors. Taking reciprocals gives (6).

For a prime \(p\), let \(t=v_p(q)\). The summand in (3) vanishes unless \(m\) is squarefree. The choice to include \(p\) in such an \(m\) contributes
\(-p^{\min(2,t)-2}\), and is allowed precisely when
\(p^{\min(2,t)}\mid l\). Thus the local factor in \(qg(q,l)\) is
\[
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-2},&t=0,\\
1,&t=1,\ p\nmid l,\\
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
1,&t\geq2,\ p^2\nmid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l.
\end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
This Euler expansion is justified by the absolute convergence of (3); equivalently, expand over finitely many primes and pass to the absolutely convergent series. The divisibility conditions in (7) also apply to \(l=0\).

If some \(p^2\) divides both \(q\) and \(l\), (7) gives \(g(q,l)=0\). In every other case, combining (6) and (7) gives exactly
\[
g(q,l)=\frac cq
\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}
\prod_{\substack{p\parallel q\\p\mid l}}(1-p^{-1}).
\tag{8}
\]
Every local factor in (7) lies in \([0,1]\). Their product therefore lies in \([0,1]\), proving
\[
0\leq g(q,l)\leq\frac1q.
\tag{9}
\]

## The finite second-moment identity

Let
\[
L(r)=\varphi(r)G(r)^2,
\qquad \lambda(r)=c^2L(r).
\]
The function \(L\) is multiplicative. Its prime-power values are
\[
L(p)=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{p(p-1)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^j)=0\quad(j\geq3).
\tag{10}
\]
These formulas follow from counting the \(p^j-p^{j-1}\) residues coprime to \(p^j\); multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) follows from the Chinese remainder theorem.

For \(t\geq1\), define a function on residues modulo \(p^t\) by
\[
b_{p,t}(l)=
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Equations (7)--(8), including their zero cases, give
\[
qg(q,l)=c\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
(1-p^{-2})^{-1}b_{p,t}(l).
\tag{11}
\]
For \(t=1\), there are \(p-1\) residues with \(b_{p,1}=1\) and one with \(b_{p,1}=1-p^{-1}\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1p\sum_{l\bmod p}b_{p,1}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-2}
\left(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^3}\right)\\
&=\frac{p^4-2p^2+p}{(p^2-1)^2}\\
&=1+\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2}=1+L(p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
For \(t\geq2\), precisely \(p^{t-2}\) of the \(p^t\) residues have \(b_{p,t}=0\), and the other \(p^t-p^{t-2}\) have value one. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1{p^t}
\sum_{l\bmod p^t}b_{p,t}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\\
&=1+\frac1{p^2-1}\\
&=1+L(p)+L(p^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
The last equality uses
\((p-1)+p(p-1)=p^2-1\).

The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the \(q\) residues modulo \(q\) with the Cartesian product of the residue sets modulo its prime-power factors. Averaging the square of (11) consequently factors into the local averages (12)--(13). With empty products understood when \(q=1\), this yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
q\sum_{l=1}^qg(q,l)^2
&=\frac1q\sum_{l=1}^q(qg(q,l))^2\\
&=c^2\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^tL(p^j)\right)\\
&=c^2\sum_{r\mid q}L(r)
=\sum_{r\mid q}\lambda(r).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]

## Absolute summability and explicit tail estimates

The support of \(L\) consists of integers with no prime exponent exceeding two. Every such integer has a unique representation
\[
r=ab^2,
\qquad a,b\text{ squarefree},\quad(a,b)=1.
\tag{15}
\]
For every prime \(p\geq2\), set
\[
A_p=\frac{p^3}{(p-1)(p+1)^2}.
\]
The denominator minus the numerator equals \(p^2-p-1\), which is at least one for \(p\geq2\). Thus \(0<A_p\leq1\), and (10) becomes
\[
L(p)=\frac{A_p}{p^3},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{A_p}{p^2}.
\]
Multiplying these inequalities over the prime factors in (15) proves
\[
0\leq\lambda(ab^2)\leq\frac{c^2}{a^3b^2}.
\tag{16}
\]
Dropping the restrictions on \(a,b\) only increases these nonnegative sums. In particular
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
\leq c^2\left(\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-3}\right)
\left(\sum_{b\geq1}b^{-2}\right)
\leq3c^2<\infty,
\tag{17}
\]
where the two series are bounded by
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}dt=3/2\) and
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt=2\), respectively.

We can now evaluate the sum by its absolutely convergent Euler product. Equation (10) gives
\[
1+L(p)+L(p^2)
=1+\frac1{p^2-1}=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}.
\]
Consequently (6) implies
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
=c^2\prod_p(1+L(p)+L(p^2))
=c^2\zeta(2)=c.
\tag{18}
\]

For every real \(T>0\), we have the explicit bound
\[
\sum_{b>T}\frac1{b^2}\leq\frac2T.
\tag{19}
\]
For \(T\geq1\), putting \(N=\lfloor T\rfloor\geq T/2\) bounds this infinite tail by
\(\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N\leq2/T\).
For \(0<T<1\), the sum is at most \(2\), which is at most \(2/T\).
For any \(R>0\), (16) and then (19), with \(T=\sqrt{R/a}\), give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{a\geq1}\frac1{a^3}
\sum_{b>\sqrt{R/a}}\frac1{b^2}\\
&\leq2c^2R^{-1/2}\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}\\
&\leq\frac{10}{3}R^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
\]
For each \(a\), the inner infinite sum before summation over \(a\) is at most \(2\sqrt{a/R}\). Its contribution after multiplication by \(c^2a^{-3}\) is at most \(2c^2R^{-1/2}a^{-5/2}\). The final bound uses \(c\leq1\) and
\[
\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}
\leq1+\int_1^\infty t^{-5/2}dt=\frac53.
\tag{21}
\]

Multiplication of (16) by \(ab^2\) gives
\(ab^2\lambda(ab^2)\leq c^2a^{-2}\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}\frac1{a^2}
\sum_{1\leq b\leq\sqrt{R/a}}1\\
&\leq c^2R^{1/2}\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}a^{-5/2}
\leq\frac53R^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
\]
For each \(a\leq R\), the inner sum has
\(\lfloor\sqrt{R/a}\rfloor\leq\sqrt{R/a}\) terms, each contributing at most \(c^2a^{-2}\). Its total is at most \(c^2R^{1/2}a^{-5/2}\). Summing over the \(\lfloor R\rfloor\) possible values of \(a\), and applying (21), gives the last inequality in (22).

For \(R\geq2\), \(\log(2R)\geq\log4>1\). Therefore (20) and (22) imply both bounds requested in the statement, with the same absolute constant \(C=10/3\). They also prove the stronger versions without logarithmic factors.

## The Ramanujan series

There are \(\varphi(r)\) terms in the defining sum for \(c_r(n)\), each of absolute value one. Hence, for every integer \(n\),
\[
|c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
\sum_{r\geq1}|\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)|
\leq\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)=c.
\tag{23}
\]
This proves absolute convergence, with a bound uniform in \(n\).

For completeness, the multiplicativity needed to evaluate the series follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem. If \((s,t)=1\), choose integers \(u,v\) with \(tu\equiv1\pmod s\) and \(sv\equiv1\pmod t\). A unit residue \(a\pmod{st}\) corresponding to unit residues \(b\pmod s\), \(d\pmod t\) satisfies
\[
\frac{a}{st}\equiv\frac{bu}{s}+\frac{dv}{t}\pmod1.
\]
Summing the resulting exponential identity over \(b,d\), and using the permutations of unit residues induced by multiplication by \(u,v\), gives
\[
c_{st}(n)=c_s(n)c_t(n).
\tag{24}
\]

The finite geometric sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{a=1}^k e(an/k)=k\,\boldsymbol1_{k\mid n}.
\]
Subtracting the term for the zero residue modulo \(p\) gives
\(c_p(n)=p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}-1\).
Subtracting the sum over residues divisible by \(p\) from the full sum modulo \(p^2\) gives
\[
c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}
-p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}.
\]
Adding these two exact identities yields
\[
c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
\tag{25}
\]
By (23)--(24), the absolutely convergent series has the Euler expansion
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)
=c^2\prod_p
\left(1+\frac{c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)}{(p^2-1)^2}\right).
\tag{26}
\]
Using (6), absorb the factor \((1-p^{-2})^2\) of \(c^2\) into each local factor. If \(p^2\nmid n\), (25) gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1-\frac1{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{(p^2-1)^2-1}{p^4}
=1-\frac2{p^2}.
\tag{27}
\]
If \(p^2\mid n\), it gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1+\frac{p^2-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2}
=1-\frac1{p^2}.
\tag{28}
\]
All these product operations are legitimate: (26) is justified by absolute convergence, and (6) converges. The product \(\prod_p(1-2/p^2)\) converges to a positive number as well. Indeed, for \(0\leq u\leq1/2\),
\(-\log(1-u)=\int_0^u(1-t)^{-1}dt\leq2u\), so
\(\sum_p|\log(1-2/p^2)|\leq4\sum_p p^{-2}<\infty\).

Finally, when \(n\geq1\), only finitely many primes satisfy \(p^2\mid n\). Replacing the factors (27) by (28) for those primes multiplies the baseline product by
\[
\frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.
\]
Thus (26) equals precisely
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\mathfrak S(n)=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
\prod_{p^2\mid n}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.}
\]
This proves every assertion of P1.

No numerical checks or external sources were used.

# Assembly of P1–P7

Integrator's report. Inputs: `problem.md`, `plan.json`, `props/P1..P7/{statement,proof}.md`,
`results.json`. The only external text I opened was the supplied
`papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf` (J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan,
T. D. Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers*, Phil. Trans. R. Soc.
Lond. A 356 (1998) 739–761, doi:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183). I used it only to confirm
that P2 quotes Lemma 2.2 correctly; the quotation is accurate. I did not access
any excluded author, the excluded paper, GitLab, other runs or post-2010 sources.
My scripts are in `scripts/` (`constants.py`, `profile.py`).

Notation: $c=\zeta(2)^{-1}$, $d=\deg f$, $a=4d-1$, $\theta=2d/a$,
$\eta=\eta_d=\min\{1/5,1/a\}$, $Y=f(y)$. $W_f$, $D_f$, $R_f$, $B_f$, $K_f$, $\Theta_f$ and $F_f$
are as in P7. Their definitions in P4, P5, P6 and P7 agree verbatim; the
identifications between them are listed in §2.

## 1. Explicit composition

Fix $0<\varepsilon<\eta/2$ and put $\delta=\varepsilon/2$. Take $x\ge x_0(f)$, so that
$Z:=x^\theta\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}$ and $R:=x^{2/a}\ge 2$. Let $z\ge1$ be the
unique real number with $f(z)=Z$; it exists because $f'\ge1$.

**Case $Y\ge Z$.** Then $z\le y$, and exactly
$V_f(x,y)=V_f(x,z)+V_f(x;z,y)$.

*Step 1 (P2, first part, exponent $\delta$).* This step needs
$x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ and $Z\le Y\le x$:
$$V_f(x;z,y)=cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)+O_{f,\varepsilon}\big(x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}\big).$$

*Step 2 (P3, exponent $\delta$).* For $z<k\le y$ and $1\le h\le x/f(k)$, the
number $m=hf(k)$ is an integer in $[1,x]$, so P3 applies to it. There are
$\le x/f(k)$ values of $h$, and $f'(k)/f(k)\ll_f 1/k$, $y\ll_f x^{1/d}$. Hence
$$S_f=M+O_{f,\varepsilon}\big(x^{9/5+\delta}\log 2x\big),\qquad
M:=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{h\le x/f(k)}(x-hf(k))\,\mathfrak S(hf(k)).$$

*Step 3 (P4).* This step needs $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$, $Z\le Y\le x$ and $2\le R\le x$. With
$A=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}\log^2(2R)+R^{-1/2}\log^2(2R)\log(2x)$:
$$T_f=R_f\log(Y/Z)+O_f(A),\qquad M=I+O_f(x^2A),\quad I:=\int_Z^Y\sum_{h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt .$$
P4's coefficient is $\sum_r\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r$. P5 shows that it equals $P_f(1)=\operatorname{Res}_{s=1}D_f$, which is the
$R_f$ of P6 and P7.

*Step 4 (P6 integral identity; needs $2\le Z\le Y\le x$).* Exactly,
$2I=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)$. From the definition of $F_f$, the
following identity also holds exactly:
$$x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)=-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).$$
I re-derived both identities. The $B_f$ terms cancel, and the $cx(Y-Z)$
from P2 is matched by the $c/H$ term of $F_f$.

*Steps 1–4 combined.* The errors from Step 3 are multiplied by $2$ (on $S_f$)
and by $x^2$ (on $T_f$). This gives
$$\Big|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)\Big|\ll_{f,\varepsilon}
x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5+\delta}\log 2x+x^2A. \tag{$*$}$$

*Step 5 (boundary terms).*
- P2, second part, at $z$: $0\le V_f(x,z)\ll_{f,\varepsilon} x^{1+\delta}Z^{2-1/d}=x^{2-1/a+\delta}$, since $1+\theta(2-1/d)=2-1/a$.
- P6, using $|F_f(H)|\ll_f H^{-3/2}$ for $H\ge1$: $x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\ll_f x^{1/2}Z^{3/2}=x^{1/2+3d/a}\le x^{2-1/a}$, because $(2-1/a)-(1/2+3d/a)=(6d-5)/(2a)>0$.

*Step 6 (bounding each error term).* With $Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a}$:

| term | bound | uses |
|---|---|---|
| $x^{3/2+\delta}$ | $\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$ | $\eta\le 1/5<1/2$ |
| $xY^{1-1/d}$ | $\le x^{2-1/d}\le x^{2-\eta}$ | $Y\le x$, $\eta\le 1/a\le 1/d$ |
| $x^{9/5+\delta}\log 2x$ | $\ll_\varepsilon x^{9/5+\varepsilon}\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$ | $\eta\le1/5$ (**this is the source of the cap $1/5$**) |
| $x^2A$ | $\ll x^{2-1/a}\log^3 2x\ll_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$ | $\eta\le 1/a$ |
| $V_f(x,z)$ | $\ll x^{2-1/a+\delta}$ | $\eta\le 1/a$ |
| $x^2\lvert F_f(x/Z)\rvert$ | $\ll x^{2-1/a}$ | Step 5 |

Therefore $|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|\ll_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$.

**Case $Y<Z$.**
- P2, second part, at $y$: $V_f(x,y)\ll x^{1+\delta}Y^{2-1/d}\le x^{2-1/a+\delta}$.
- P6: $x^2|F_f(x/Y)|\ll x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\le x^{2-1/a}$.

The triangle inequality gives the same bound $x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$.

**Power main term.** By P6, $|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|\le C_fH^{-13/8}$ for $H=x/Y\ge1$. Multiplying by $x^2$:
$$|x^2F_f(x/Y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}|\le C_f\,x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}.$$
Combined with the profile estimate:
$$|V_f(x,y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}|\ll_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}+x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}.$$

**Corollary in the plan.** Take $0<\delta'<\eta/3$, $x^{1-2\eta/3+\delta'}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta'}$ and $\varepsilon=\delta'$
(admissible, since $\delta'<\eta/2$). The two relative errors are:
- $x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}/(x^{1/2}Y^{3/2})=(Y/x)^{1/8}\le x^{-\delta'/8}$;
- $x^{2-\eta+\delta'}/(x^{1/2}Y^{3/2})\le x^{-\delta'/2}\le x^{-\delta'/8}$.

Since $K_f>0$ (P5), this gives $|V_f/(K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2})-1|\ll_{f,\delta'}x^{-\delta'/8}$ for $x\ge x_0$.

All constants depend only on $f$ and $\varepsilon$. **The propositions compose to the plan's main theorem exactly, with no loss.**

Explicit exponents:

| $d$ | $\eta_d$ | where $V_f\sim K_f x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$ is guaranteed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1/5$ | $x^{13/15+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ |
| 2 | $1/7$ | $x^{19/21+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ |
| 3 | $1/11$ | $x^{31/33+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ |

## 2. Interface check

Each item below is a hypothesis of one proposition, checked at the point where P7 uses it:

- **P2 ranges.** P2 needs $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ and $Z\le Y\le x$, with real $z,y$. P7's $z$ is real with $f(z)=x^\theta$, and $z\le y$ by monotonicity. The initial-modulus bound needs $z\ge1$ and $f(z)\le x$; P7 also applies it at $z=y$ when $Y<Z$. ✓
- **P3 range.** P3 needs an integer $1\le m\le x$ and is uniform in $m$, including when $x-m$ is bounded. P7 uses $m=hf(k)$ with $h\le x/f(k)$. ✓ P3 proves the stronger bound $x^{4/5}$, which has no $\varepsilon$. It lists P1 as a dependency but does not use it; this is harmless.
- **P3 and P4 definitions.** The definitions of $C_x$ and $\mathfrak S$ are identical in P2, P3 and P4. ✓
- **P4 ranges.** P4 needs $2\le R\le x$ and $2\le Z$; the latter follows from $f(1)\ge2$. P7's choice $R=x^{2/a}$ satisfies both once $x\ge x_0$. The $Z^{-1/d}$ in $A$ comes from a factor $1/z$, valid for real $z$. ✓
- **P4/P5 constant.** P4 defines $R_f=\sum\lambda\rho/r$, with $\lambda=c^2\varphi\prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2}$, which equals P1's $\varphi\gamma^2$. P6 and P7 define $R_f$ as $\operatorname{Res}_{s=1}D_f$. P5 proves that both equal $P_f(1)$. ✓
- **$B_f$.** P5 gives $B_f=(\gamma_E-3/2)R_f+P_f'(1)$, and P6 and P7 use the Laurent definition; P5 (26) proves they agree. In any case $B_f$ cancels in the assembly.
- **$K_f$.** P5 gives $K_f=-\tfrac83\zeta(-\tfrac12)H_f(-\tfrac12)$, and P6 and P7 use $-\tfrac{16}3\operatorname{Res}_{-1/2}D_f$. They agree, because the residue of $\zeta(2s+2)$ at $s=-\tfrac12$ is $\tfrac12$. ✓
- **$D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))$.** P5 states this and P6 uses it to produce the $+cH$ term. ✓
- **P5→P6 uniformity (minor, not a defect).** P5 bounds $H_f$ only on each fixed vertical line ($C(f,\sigma)$). P6 needs a bound that is uniform on the strip $-5/8\le\sigma\le2$. P6 proves this itself from the Euler product (its eq. (9)) and does not rely on P5 for it. The contour line $\Re s=-5/8$ lies inside P5's region of continuation, $\Re s>-3/4$. ✓
- **P6 ranges.** The bound $|F_f-K_fH^{-3/2}|\le CH^{-13/8}$ holds for all real $H\ge1$; P7 uses it at $H=x/Y$ and $H=x/Z$, both $\ge1$. The integral identity needs $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. ✓
- **External input.** P2 uses BGPVW Lemma 2.2 with $k=2$ and $1\le Q\le x$, which states $\Upsilon_2(x,Q)\ll x^{1+\varepsilon}Q$. I checked the PDF: the quotation is exact. P2 also correctly checks that the source's normalisation of $E$ matches ours and that all residue classes are included.

No proposition is used with a range, uniformity or error term other than the one it states. Two points are cosmetic only: the P3 dependency that is listed but unused, and the strip uniformity that P6 supplies itself rather than taking from P5.

## 3. Numerics

I recomputed the constants independently (`scripts/constants.py`), with Euler products over $p\le10^7$ plus a tail correction. The values agree with those from $p\le10^6$ to 7 digits.

| $f$ | $R_f$ | $B_f$ | $H_f(-1/2)$ | $K_f$ | `constant_extrapolated` | rel. discrepancy $(K_f-C)/C$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | 0.3923477 | −0.4368427 | 0.2490833 | **0.1380826** | 0.134475 ± 0.007285 | **+2.68 %** (0.50 of the band) |
| $k^3+2$ | 0.3953324 | −0.4418196 | 0.2446185 | **0.1356075** | 0.136321 ± 0.002404 | **−0.52 %** (0.30 of the band) |
| $2k+1$ (extra) | 0.3786969 | −0.4242357 | 0.2572561 | 0.1426133 | 0.141686 ± 0.008218 | +0.65 % |

These match the plan's values (0.138083, 0.135608, 0.142613). None of the discrepancies is close to a clean factor.

**Diagnosing the extrapolation.** I fitted the snapshot's own model, $N(r)=C+a\sqrt r+br$, to the eight largest-$x$ ratios. I did this once on the data and once on the **exact predicted profile** $N_{\rm pred}(r)=F_f(H)H^{3/2}$ at $H=x/Y$ (`scripts/profile.py`). Intercepts:

| $f$ | fit to data | fit to predicted profile | true limit $K_f$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | 0.134475 | 0.134364 | 0.138083 |
| $k^3+2$ | 0.136321 | 0.135793 | 0.135608 |
| $2k+1$ | 0.141686 | 0.141685 | 0.142613 |

Applied to the predicted profile, the fit model reproduces the snapshot's intercepts to within 0.08 %, 0.4 % and 0.001 %. So the 2.7 % gap for $k^2+1$ is bias in the three-term model, not an error in $K_f$. The profile approaches $K_f$ slowly: at $H=200,400,700,1000$, $N_{\rm pred}$ for $k^2+1$ is 0.14024, 0.13963, 0.13891, 0.13877.

**Direct profile comparison** at $x=2.56\cdot10^8$, $(N_{\rm data}/N_{\rm pred}-1)$ over the eight ratios plus the diagnostic ratio 0.005:

| $f$ | range of $N_{\rm data}/N_{\rm pred}-1$ | trend from $x=1.28\cdot10^8$ to $2.56\cdot10^8$ |
|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | +0.007 % to +0.10 % | decreasing at most ratios |

- $x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}/(x^{1/2}Y^{3/2})=(Y/x)^{1/8}\le x^{-\delta'/8}$;
- $x^{2-\eta+\delta'}/(x^{1/2}Y^{3/2})\le x^{-\delta'/2}\le x^{-\delta'/8}$.

Since $K_f>0$ (P5), this gives $|V_f/(K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2})-1|\ll_{f,\delta'}x^{-\delta'/8}$ for $x\ge x_0$.

All constants depend only on $f$ and $\varepsilon$. **The propositions compose to the plan's main theorem exactly, with no loss.**

Explicit exponents:

| $d$ | $\eta_d$ | where $V_f\sim K_f x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$ is guaranteed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $1/5$ | $x^{13/15+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ |
| 2 | $1/7$ | $x^{19/21+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ |
| 3 | $1/11$ | $x^{31/33+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ |

## 2. Interface check

Each item below is a hypothesis of one proposition, checked at the point where P7 uses it:

- **P2 ranges.** P2 needs $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ and $Z\le Y\le x$, with real $z,y$. P7's $z$ is real with $f(z)=x^\theta$, and $z\le y$ by monotonicity. The initial-modulus bound needs $z\ge1$ and $f(z)\le x$; P7 also applies it at $z=y$ when $Y<Z$. ✓
- **P3 range.** P3 needs an integer $1\le m\le x$ and is uniform in $m$, including when $x-m$ is bounded. P7 uses $m=hf(k)$ with $h\le x/f(k)$. ✓ P3 proves the stronger bound $x^{4/5}$, which has no $\varepsilon$. It lists P1 as a dependency but does not use it; this is harmless.
- **P3 and P4 definitions.** The definitions of $C_x$ and $\mathfrak S$ are identical in P2, P3 and P4. ✓
- **P4 ranges.** P4 needs $2\le R\le x$ and $2\le Z$; the latter follows from $f(1)\ge2$. P7's choice $R=x^{2/a}$ satisfies both once $x\ge x_0$. The $Z^{-1/d}$ in $A$ comes from a factor $1/z$, valid for real $z$. ✓
- **P4/P5 constant.** P4 defines $R_f=\sum\lambda\rho/r$, with $\lambda=c^2\varphi\prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2}$, which equals P1's $\varphi\gamma^2$. P6 and P7 define $R_f$ as $\operatorname{Res}_{s=1}D_f$. P5 proves that both equal $P_f(1)$. ✓
- **$B_f$.** P5 gives $B_f=(\gamma_E-3/2)R_f+P_f'(1)$, and P6 and P7 use the Laurent definition; P5 (26) proves they agree. In any case $B_f$ cancels in the assembly.
- **$K_f$.** P5 gives $K_f=-\tfrac83\zeta(-\tfrac12)H_f(-\tfrac12)$, and P6 and P7 use $-\tfrac{16}3\operatorname{Res}_{-1/2}D_f$. They agree, because the residue of $\zeta(2s+2)$ at $s=-\tfrac12$ is $\tfrac12$. ✓
- **$D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))$.** P5 states this and P6 uses it to produce the $+cH$ term. ✓
- **P5→P6 uniformity (minor, not a defect).** P5 bounds $H_f$ only on each fixed vertical line ($C(f,\sigma)$). P6 needs a bound that is uniform on the strip $-5/8\le\sigma\le2$. P6 proves this itself from the Euler product (its eq. (9)) and does not rely on P5 for it. The contour line $\Re s=-5/8$ lies inside P5's region of continuation, $\Re s>-3/4$. ✓
- **P6 ranges.** The bound $|F_f-K_fH^{-3/2}|\le CH^{-13/8}$ holds for all real $H\ge1$; P7 uses it at $H=x/Y$ and $H=x/Z$, both $\ge1$. The integral identity needs $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. ✓
- **External input.** P2 uses BGPVW Lemma 2.2 with $k=2$ and $1\le Q\le x$, which states $\Upsilon_2(x,Q)\ll x^{1+\varepsilon}Q$. I checked the PDF: the quotation is exact. P2 also correctly checks that the source's normalisation of $E$ matches ours and that all residue classes are included.

No proposition is used with a range, uniformity or error term other than the one it states. Two points are cosmetic only: the P3 dependency that is listed but unused, and the strip uniformity that P6 supplies itself rather than taking from P5.

## 3. Numerics

I recomputed the constants independently (`scripts/constants.py`), with Euler products over $p\le10^7$ plus a tail correction. The values agree with those from $p\le10^6$ to 7 digits.

| $f$ | $R_f$ | $B_f$ | $H_f(-1/2)$ | $K_f$ | `constant_extrapolated` | rel. discrepancy $(K_f-C)/C$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | 0.3923477 | −0.4368427 | 0.2490833 | **0.1380826** | 0.134475 ± 0.007285 | **+2.68 %** (0.50 of the band) |
| $k^3+2$ | 0.3953324 | −0.4418196 | 0.2446185 | **0.1356075** | 0.136321 ± 0.002404 | **−0.52 %** (0.30 of the band) |
| $2k+1$ (extra) | 0.3786969 | −0.4242357 | 0.2572561 | 0.1426133 | 0.141686 ± 0.008218 | +0.65 % |

These match the plan's values (0.138083, 0.135608, 0.142613). None of the discrepancies is close to a clean factor.

**Diagnosing the extrapolation.** I fitted the snapshot's own model, $N(r)=C+a\sqrt r+br$, to the eight largest-$x$ ratios. I did this once on the data and once on the **exact predicted profile** $N_{\rm pred}(r)=F_f(H)H^{3/2}$ at $H=x/Y$ (`scripts/profile.py`). Intercepts:

| $f$ | fit to data | fit to predicted profile | true limit $K_f$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | 0.134475 | 0.134364 | 0.138083 |
| $k^3+2$ | 0.136321 | 0.135793 | 0.135608 |
| $2k+1$ | 0.141686 | 0.141685 | 0.142613 |

Applied to the predicted profile, the fit model reproduces the snapshot's intercepts to within 0.08 %, 0.4 % and 0.001 %. So the 2.7 % gap for $k^2+1$ is bias in the three-term model, not an error in $K_f$. The profile approaches $K_f$ slowly: at $H=200,400,700,1000$, $N_{\rm pred}$ for $k^2+1$ is 0.14024, 0.13963, 0.13891, 0.13877.

**Direct profile comparison** at $x=2.56\cdot10^8$, $(N_{\rm data}/N_{\rm pred}-1)$ over the eight ratios plus the diagnostic ratio 0.005:

| $f$ | range of $N_{\rm data}/N_{\rm pred}-1$ | trend from $x=1.28\cdot10^8$ to $2.56\cdot10^8$ |
|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | +0.007 % to +0.10 % | decreasing at most ratios |
| $k^3+2$ | −0.02 % to +2.2 % | decreasing at 7 of 9 ratios |
| $2k+1$ | ≤ 0.0005 % | — |

For $k^3+2$, $y$ is small (86–635), so the $k$-sampling terms (the $Z^{-1/d}$ terms in P4) are large at this $x$. The theorem's error bound $x^{2-1/11}$ is not small at $x\approx 2.6\cdot10^8$; relative to the main term it is $\approx x^{-1/11}r^{-3/2}$. The numerics are therefore consistent with the theorem but cannot test its error exponent.

## 4. Final theorem (what P1–P7 prove)

Let $f\in\mathbb Z[t]$ with $\deg f=d\ge1$, $f(t)\ge2$ and $f'(t)\ge1$ for $t\ge1$; no irreducibility or squarefreeness condition is needed. Put $Y=f(y)$ and $\eta_d=\min\{1/5,1/(4d-1)\}$. Define
$$W_f(h)=\prod_p(1-2p^{-2})\Big[1+\rho(p^{j})/(p^{j}(p^2-2))\Big],\qquad j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\},$$
and
$$\Theta_f(H)=\sum_{h\le H}W_f(h)(H-h)^2/h,\qquad F_f(H)=R_f\log H+B_f+1/(\zeta(2)H)-\Theta_f(H)/H^2,$$
where $R_f$ and $B_f$ are the residue and the shifted constant term of $D_f(s)=\sum W_f(h)h^{-s}$ at $s=1$. Let $K_f=-\tfrac83\zeta(-\tfrac12)H_f(-\tfrac12)>0$, with $H_f$ the Euler product of P5.

Then for $0<\varepsilon<\eta_d/2$, uniformly for $x\ge x_0(f,\varepsilon)$ and real $y\ge1$ with $Y\le x$:
$$V_f(x,y)=x^2F_f(x/Y)+O_{f,\varepsilon}(x^{2-\eta_d+\varepsilon}),$$
$$V_f(x,y)=K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}+O_{f,\varepsilon}(x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}+x^{2-\eta_d+\varepsilon}).$$
Consequently, $V_f\sim K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$ with relative error $\ll x^{-\delta/8}$ for $x^{1-2\eta_d/3+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$.

This is exactly the plan's main theorem; there is no loss.

structured_output.final_theorem: Let f ∈ Z[t] have degree d ≥ 1, with f(t) ≥ 2 and f'(t) ≥ 1 for t ≥ 1. No irreducibility or squarefreeness assumption is needed. Put Y = f(y) and η_d = min{1/5, 1/(4d−1)}. Define W_f(h) = ∏_p (1−2/p²)[1 + ρ(p^j)/(p^j(p²−2))], where j = max{2−v_p(h), 0}, and let D_f(s) = Σ W_f(h) h^{−s}. Let R_f = Res_{s=1} D_f and B_f = lim_{s→1}[D_f(s) − R_f/(s−1)] − 3R_f/2. Put Θ_f(H) = Σ_{h≤H} W_f(h)(H−h)²/h and F_f(H) = R_f log H + B_f + 1/(ζ(2)H) − Θ_f(H)/H². Finally K_f = −(8/3)ζ(−1/2)H_f(−1/2) > 0, where H_f(s) = ∏_p (1−2/p²)(1−p^{−2s−2})B_p(s) is the Euler product of P5. Then for every 0 < ε < η_d/2, uniformly for x ≥ x_0(f,ε) and real y ≥ 1 with Y ≤ x: V_f(x,y) = x²F_f(x/Y) + O_{f,ε}(x^{2−η_d+ε}), and V_f(x,y) = K_f x^{1/2} Y^{3/2} + O_{f,ε}(x^{3/8} Y^{13/8} + x^{2−η_d+ε}). In particular, for fixed 0 < δ < η_d/3 and x^{1−2η_d/3+δ} ≤ Y ≤ x^{1−δ}, we have V_f/(K_f x^{1/2} Y^{3/2}) = 1 + O_{f,δ}(x^{−δ/8}). Concretely: η = 1/5 for d = 1, 1/7 for d = 2 and 1/11 for d = 3. Numerically K_{k²+1} ≈ 0.1380826 and K_{k³+2} ≈ 0.1356075.
interface_mismatches: No substantive mismatch: every proposition is used within its stated range, uniformity and error term (checked one by one in assembly.md §2).
Cosmetic: P3 lists P1 as a dependency but its proof does not use it. P3 proves the stronger x^{4/5} bound with no ε, and P7 uses the weaker x^{4/5+ε}.

Minor: P5 bounds H_f only on each fixed vertical line, but P6's contour shift needs a bound that is uniform on the strip −5/8 ≤ σ ≤ 2. P6 proves this bound itself from the Euler product (its eq. (9)), so the composition does not rely on anything P5 leaves out. The line Re s = −5/8 lies inside P5's region of continuation, Re s > −3/4.

Definitions are consistent across propositions. P4's R_f = Σλρ/r equals Res_{s=1} D_f = P_f(1) (P5). P5's two descriptions of B_f agree, and B_f cancels in the assembly anyway. P5's K_f = −(8/3)ζ(−1/2)H_f(−1/2) equals −(16/3)Res_{−1/2} D_f (P6/P7). D_f(0) = −1/(2ζ(2)) yields the +cH term, which cancels P2's cx(Y−Z).
External input checked: P2's quotation of BGPVW (1998) Lemma 2.2, Υ_2(x,Q) ≪ x^{1+ε}Q for 1 ≤ Q ≤ x, matches the supplied PDF exactly.
structured_output.numerics_comparison: I recomputed the constants independently, with Euler products over p ≤ 10^7 and a tail correction; they agree with the p ≤ 10^6 values to 7 digits. k²+1: K_f = 0.1380826 vs constant_extrapolated 0.134475 ± 0.007285, a relative discrepancy of +2.68% (half the band). k³+2: K_f = 0.1356075 vs 0.136321 ± 0.002404, a discrepancy of −0.52%. Check case 2k+1: 0.1426133 vs 0.141686, +0.65%. None of these is a clean factor. To diagnose the extrapolation, I applied the snapshot's own fit model N(r) = C + a√r + br, over the same eight largest-x ratios, to the exact predicted profile N_pred = F_f(H)H^{3/2} at H = x/Y. It gives intercepts 0.134364, 0.135793 and 0.141685, against the data fits 0.134475, 0.136321 and 0.141686. So the extrapolated constants are biased by the fit model, and the 2.7% gap for k²+1 is fully explained by that bias, not by an error in K_f. The profile converges slowly: for k²+1, N_pred = 0.14024 at H = 200 and 0.13877 at H = 1000. Direct comparison of V with x²F_f(x/Y) at x = 2.56e8: k²+1 agrees to 0.007–0.10%; 2k+1 to ≤ 0.0005%; k³+2 to −0.02% to +2.2%. For k³+2, y is small (86–635), and the deviation shrinks from x = 1.28e8 to 2.56e8 at 7 of the 9 ratios. This fits large k-sampling lower-order terms, but that explanation is not proved.
